1017-the-soul-of-man-under-socialism:
Oscar Wilde argues in this essay that socialism, rightly grasped, would free each person to grow into himself instead of living for others. Once machines did the dull work and no man starved, he says, men could stop posing as philanthropists and start becoming artists of their own lives.

Wilde scorns charity that props up a sick system and praises a state that leaves the soul alone. His case is witty, grand, and deliberately provoking, and it ties his love of art to a plea for human freedom. The essay still sparks debate on work, wealth, and what a good life is for.
10970-pragmatism:
D. L. Murray wrote this short introduction to pragmatism for the Philosophies Ancient and Modern series, with a preface by F. C. S. Schiller. Murray rejects caricatures of pragmatism as a revolt against logic, a Wild West import, or Anglo-Saxon commercialism. He presents it instead as a modern answer to old puzzles about knowledge, belief, and truth.

Chapters trace the genesis of pragmatism, the will to believe, and the test of ideas by their practical value. A yard measure beats the eye for size, Murray notes, and bread nourishes better than stone, even without absolute certainty. The book suits readers new to philosophy who want a clear, brief account of why pragmatists judge beliefs by what they do in life.
11142-unitarianism:
W. G. Tarrant wrote this 1912 history of Unitarianism, published in London. Tarrant opens by explaining terms: the chief issue between Trinitarians and Unitarians concerns the relation of Jesus Christ to God. Trinitarian dogma, as in the Athanasian Creed, presents three Persons in one God, while Arius held the Son of similar, not same, substance with the Father.

Chapters follow the earlier movement in England, from Unitarian martyrs and old Nonconformists to the Unitarian Tracts, then New England before the Great Awakening and the liberal reaction. Dr. Richard Price, an Arian to the last, still helped organise Unitarian forces. The book gives a clear, compact account of a liberal tradition for general readers and students of religion.
15681-constructive-imperialism:
Five speeches on empire and reform by Viscount Milner, delivered in the autumn of 1907 and printed in London in 1908. Milner, a leading Unionist voice, spoke at Tunbridge Wells, Guildford, Edinburgh, Rugby, and Oxford. Each speech takes one theme and presses it as policy, not mere sentiment. The National Review Office issued the set as a compact party text.

Tariff reform opens the book, followed by a plea for a constructive policy across the empire. Unionists and the empire, Unionists and social reform, and sweated industries complete the arc. Milner links imperial unity to better wages, housing, and work at home. The speeches matter as a clear statement of Edwardian imperialism with a social conscience.
16076-preaching-and-paganism:
Albert Parker Fitch, professor of religion at Amherst, gave these Yale lectures in 1920 as the forty-sixth Lyman Beecher series on preaching. Published by Yale University Press on the Cooper memorial fund, the book asks how Christian preaching can speak to a modern, pagan-minded world. Chapters move from the learner, the doer, and the seer to the children of Zion and the sons of Greece.

Later lectures weigh eating, drinking, and being merry, the gulf between faith and doubt, grace and knowledge, and worship as the chief path to God. Fitch writes as a scholar and a preacher, earnest about both pulpit and pew. Readers interested in theology, preaching, and the church in a changing age will find a thoughtful, serious work.
16309-paradoxes-of-catholicism:
Robert Hugh Benson shaped these sermons into a set of paired opposites. First preached in England, New York, and Rome, they pair peace and war, wealth and want, joy and grief, faith and reason, meekness and force, life and death. Each chapter holds two truths that seem to fight each other and shows how Catholic thought keeps both.

The book opens with Christ as both God and man, and the Church as both divine and human. Benson keeps the style plain for a sermon audience, with short chapters and clear headings. Readers get a direct, confident case for a faith that lives with tension rather than smoothing it away.
16512-an-apology-for-atheism:
Charles Southwell, writing as one of atheism's apostles, addressed this 1846 pamphlet to religious investigators of every denomination. He argues that faith bears closely on politics, and that a people held in superstition cannot win political freedom. Religious error, he claims, underlies much public injustice, though honest reformers have yet to learn it.

The pamphlet is short, bold, and polemical, printed in London by J. Watson. Southwell published it anonymously at first, in an age when such views carried real risk. For historians of freethought, it stands as a frank early Victorian case against religion's public power.
16833-auguste-comte-and-positivism:
John Stuart Mill wrote this 1865 study of Auguste Comte and positivism, in two parts, the first on Comte's Course of Positive Philosophy. Mill notes that positivism was once known only to a few direct pupils. It had grown into a mode of thought that all who weighed the great problems of the age had to meet, friend or foe.

Mill sets out Comte's system with care, then judges where it helps and where it fails. He writes for readers who want the new philosophy in plain English, not in French jargon. The book remains a key first guide to Comte, and a fine sample of Mill at his clearest, weighing a rival system with fairness and bite.
17350-the-practice-and-theory-of-bolshev:
Bertrand Russell's Practice and Theory of Bolshevism, first published in November 1920, reports a visit to Russia and then judges its creed. Part One covers what was hoped from Bolshevism, Lenin, Trotsky, and Gorky, art and education, the soviet constitution, failed industry, daily life in Moscow, town and country, and foreign policy. Part Two turns to theory: materialist history, democracy, revolution, dictatorship, and the individual.

Russell writes with sympathy for aims and skepticism about means, in clear, analytic prose. His verdict, that Russian communism had failed on its own terms, sparked fierce debate. Readers of political history will find a concise, firsthand classic of early Soviet criticism, still sharp a century on.
17416-a-critical-examination-of-socialis:
W. H. Mallock's 1908 Critical Examination of Socialism takes the theory in its earliest systematic form, as Karl Marx built it in the mid-nineteenth century. Chapters summarize Marx on labor as the sole producer of wealth, capital as past labor embodied in implements, and wages sinking under capitalism. Mallock tests each doctrine against the facts of production and distribution.

His prose is close, argumentative, and learned, with long chapter summaries for the careful reader. The book suits students of political thought and of the socialist debate before the First World War. As a period critique, it shows the anti-Marx case at its most systematic, and should be read beside Marx himself.
17452-adventures-in-criticism:
A. T. Quiller-Couch, writing weekly on books for The Speaker, gathered these short papers in New York in 1896. He dedicates the book to A. B. Walkley, who wrote on plays beside him, and notes that the pieces are reprinted with a few changes. The set ranges from Chaucer, Shakespeare's lyrics, Samuel Daniel, and William Browne to Scott, Burns, Charles Reade, Robert Louis Stevenson, and Zola.

Each essay is brief, opinionated, and meant to be read for pleasure rather than as a system. Quiller-Couch judges old and new writers side by side, praising craft and feeling over theory. Readers get a lively sample of late Victorian literary talk, useful for meeting classic authors through one sharp, friendly critic's eyes.
17556-sextus-empiricus-and-greek-sceptic:
Mary Mills Patrick wrote this study of Sextus Empiricus and Greek scepticism. It was a thesis accepted for the degree of doctor of philosophy at the University of Bern, Switzerland, in November 1897. Patrick was president of the American College at Constantinople. The book, published at Cambridge in 1899, also carries Patrick's translation from the Greek of the first book of Sextus's Pyrrhonic Sketches.

Chapters open with the historical relations of Sextus: his name, profession, time, birthplace, and the seat of the sceptical school while he led it. The position and aim of Pyrrhonic scepticism follow, with the subject matter of the Hypotyposes. Readers get a scholarly introduction to ancient scepticism, with a translation to test it by.
18168-the-heavenly-father-lectures-on-mo:
Ernest Naville wrote The Heavenly Father as lectures on modern atheism, delivered at Geneva and Lausanne before some two thousand five hundred men, and turned into English by Henry Downton. The Boston firm William V. Spencer printed the book in 1867.

Lectures run from our idea of God to life without God, the revival of atheism, and nature, each argued with calm, Swiss clarity. Naville opposes to error a faith in God as given by the Gospel, a father in heaven. The book is a thoughtful, Victorian defense of faith, and a fair window on the faith-doubt debates of its age.
18223-the-essence-of-buddhism:
Edwin Arnold introduces this little Haldeman-Julius pocket book, number 325 in the Ten Cent Pocket Series, copyrighted in 1922 at Girard, Kansas. The compiler, Mr. Bowden, gathered extracts from very various Buddhist sources into an anthology, rather than setting out a full system of Buddhist morality and doctrine. Arnold calls the pieces rubies, sapphires, and emeralds of wisdom, compassion, and human brotherhood.

Brief verses and maxims give lofty tenets of the Light of Asia in small compass, one for each day. Arnold suggests that a reader who marks the months with these simple pages may end the year a better man than he began it. Readers get Buddhism in pocket form: short sayings chosen for daily use, not a scholar's treatise.
19003-a-candid-examination-of-theism:
Writing as Physicus, the author of this 1878 essay tests belief in God by cold reason. He held the piece back for years, fearing later thought might change his views, then judged it fit to face other minds. The preface states that aim in plain terms.

Chapters weigh the case for design in nature, from Paley and Mill to general laws and the saving of energy in physics. The author finds the design case circular and presses the case from laws instead. Readers get a frank Victorian work on faith and science, arguing step by step rather than by appeal to feeling.
19192-what-is-darwinism:
Charles Hodge of Princeton wrote this 1874 book asking what Darwinism truly is. He sets the scriptural theory beside pantheism and Epicurean atoms. He sets it beside Spencer and hylozoism. He weighs each as an account of the origin of living things. The question, he argues, matters for faith and science alike.

Hodge traces Epicurus on matter, force, and motion. There blind combinations yield life and mind. He notes modern German advocates who know far more astronomy and biology. Yet they hold the same theory of the universe. Readers get a careful theological critique of Darwin, learned, firm, and of historical interest.
19468-mediaeval-socialism:
Bede Jarrett wrote this short study of medieval socialism, published in London and New York in the early nineteen hundreds. Chapters cover social conditions, the communists, the schoolmen, the lawyers, and the social reformers, closing with a theory of alms-giving.

Jarrett explains feudal order as a chain of contracts, from king through great barons down to tenants who held castle, farm, or hut in return for suit and service. The book argues that medieval thinkers faced questions of wealth and duty long before modern socialism named them. A short bibliography and an index close the study, letting readers trace the sources behind each chapter.
20248-the-necessity-of-atheism:
The Necessity of Atheism, in this 1933 printing, argues that gods began in human fear. To early man, the gods were as real as mountains and waterfalls. Spirits in drugs and wines seemed facts of the same order. Their power to heal or intoxicate proved their presence, men thought.

From such roots, the book traces belief toward doubt and reason. Its title echoes Shelley's famed student tract of the same name. Arguments cover nature, scripture, and the harm of forced belief. Readers get a blunt, clear case for unbelief from the freethought tradition.
20428-bertha-and-her-baptism:
Bertha and Her Baptism is a religious story written to teach young readers about baptism and heaven. It opens with a claim its makers held dear. Of those who have gone to heaven from this world, by far the larger part, it says, have been infants and young children.

The teaching runs through the tale of Bertha herself. Born sinners by one man's disobedience, children are born again of the Spirit, the book explains. Its early move to heaven is treated as mercy, not loss. Stories like this one filled Victorian nurseries, where faith and comfort were taught together.
21853-woman-s-work-in-the-civil-war-a-re:
Women's war work fills this 1867 record by L. P. Brockett and Mary C. Vaughan, gathered as the Civil War still raged. The gathering began in the autumn of 1863, out of a small book on the war's kind results meant for readers abroad. Henry W. Bellows of the Sanitary Commission writes the introduction. Sixteen steel engravings honor the women inside, Clara Barton among them.

The subtitle promises heroism, patriotism, and patience, and the pages deliver all three. Nurses, aid workers, teachers of freed people, and women who kept homes and farms appear in turn. Barbara Frietchie's famous defiance fronts the book. It stands as an early monument to the women the war made visible, written while their work was fresh.
21991-face-to-face-with-kaiserism:
James W. Gerard, lately America's ambassador to the German imperial court, continues his account in Face to Face with Kaiserism, published in 1918. The book follows his bestseller My Four Years in Germany, carrying the story to his return home. Gerard dedicates it to Colonel Edward M. House, statesman and friend. Facsimiles fill the plates: the Kaiser's visiting card, prison camp money, and stamps from Ruhleben camp.

Gerard shows the paper money used in prison camps and issued against German property. His subject is the system he faced for four years: the Kaiser, his court, and the machine behind them. Written while the war still raged, it is diplomacy as testimony. Gerard writes for American readers deciding what Germany under the Kaiser truly was.
22147-peter-the-hermit-a-tale-of-enthusi:
Daniel A. Goodsell, a Methodist bishop, wrote Peter the Hermit: A Tale of Enthusiasm in 1906. Peter was the ragged preacher whose sermons fired the First Crusade. Goodsell opens in the Holy Land of pilgrims' longing. The devout Christian, he writes, dreams of walking where the Master walked and praying in the garden of his agony.

From that longing Goodsell's Peter gathers his ragged army. The tale follows the march of the People's Crusade toward Jerusalem and its ruin. Goodsell treats Peter neither as saint nor fraud, but as enthusiasm made flesh. His book is part history, part sermon, aimed at church readers who loved the Crusades' great names.
22283-mind-and-motion-and-monism:
George John Romanes, Darwin's younger friend and defender, wrote Mind and Motion and Monism near the end of his life. The book appeared in 1895, after his death. Romanes quotes the old materialist claim that our feelings are only motions of matter pressing on our organs. Motion, that doctrine says, produces nothing but motion, and mind must be explained away or explained by it.

Romanes refuses the easy answer. Trained as a biologist and drawn to philosophy, he argues toward monism: mind and matter as two sides of one reality. The book joins his work on animal intelligence to the deepest question he knew. It is Victorian science thinking hard about the soul.
24186-zionism-and-anti-semitism:
This volume pairs two essays on Jewish life at the turn of the century, published in New York in 1905. Max Nordau writes on Zionism, and Gustav Gottheil writes on anti-Semitism in Europe. Nordau observes that educated readers have heard the word Zionism. Yet few, Gentile or Jew, hold a clear notion of its aims and ways. Its foes spread lies, and even its friends seldom state the whole idea plainly.

Nordau promises sober facts for readers of good faith, without exaggeration or polemical heat, about a movement that had found many adherents among Jews of all countries, above all in the East. Gottheil's essay sets beside it the hostility Jews faced in Europe. Readers get a period pair of views on a movement and the prejudice it answered.
24326-elementary-guide-to-literary-criti:
F. V. N. Painter, professor of modern languages at Roanoke College, wrote this guide to literary criticism, published by Ginn and Company in Boston in 1903. Its first part treats fundamental principles: the nature and office of criticism, the author and his work, and some aesthetic principles. The second part covers rhetorical elements: words, sentences, paragraphs, figures of speech, and style.

The third part surveys kinds of literature. It covers the nature and structure of poetry, kinds of poetry, and epic and dramatic poetry. The nature and forms of prose, essays and oratory, and the nature and classification of fiction follow. Painter opens by noting that reading serves knowledge, pleasure, and culture, and that only books of recognized excellence deserve reading, with sympathetic intelligence. Readers get a clear school guide to judging books.
24328-the-basis-of-early-christian-theis:
Lawrence Thomas Cole wrote this study to meet part of the requirements for his Doctor of Philosophy degree at Columbia University, in New York, in May 1898. Cole, a postgraduate scholar of the Church University Board of Regents, opens with a Pascal epigraph on metaphysical proofs of God, which strike few and fade within the hour. His question is what the Christian church found ready when it began to build a system of apologetics.

Chapters treat the introduction, Greek and Roman theistic arguments, the patristic point of view, patristic use of those arguments, and eclectic theism. Cole asks how far Greek philosophers advanced by speculation toward a conscious theism, and by what means they sought to prove the Divine. Readers get a learned thesis on reason, faith, and the early church.
24441-the-stoker-s-catechism:
W. J. Connor published this handbook in London and New York in 1906 for steam boiler stokers. These were men who fed coal to furnaces by hand. In his preface he notes that no books on stoking existed. A new man often learned the job in silence, afraid to ask questions lest he seem unfit for his post.

Written as questions and answers, the book covers firing, draught, coal, water, ash, and the care of boilers. It gives plain working rules a stoker could learn and use. It remains a rare, practical record of skilled manual labour in the steam age. Readers curious about how factories, ships, and railways were kept running will value it.
27197-modern-spiritualism:
Uriah Smith's Modern Spiritualism, published by the Review and Herald in 1896, treats spiritualism as a prophetic subject and a mark of the age. For nearly fifty years, Smith notes, spiritualism has been before the world, long enough to show its character by its fruits.

Smith argues that its promises, including claims to be the second coming of Christ and the portal of a golden age, fail their test. His chapters hold that the soul is not immortal, the dead are unconscious, and the agents at work are evil angels, warning readers against mediumship and its teachings.
27863-the-legacy-of-ignorantism:
Dr. T. H. Pardo de Tavera delivered this address before the Teachers Assembly at Baguio on April 23, 1920, published in Manila in 1921 in English and Spanish. He chose to speak on lay education in the public schools under the new regime ruling the Filipino people, promising to confine himself to facts.

Pardo de Tavera opens with Luke's warning to lawyers who take away the key of knowledge, then argues that rising complaints about vice show a growing moral conscience, not growing immorality. The address is a frank Filipino statement on education, morality, and the legacy of ignorance under colonial rule.
28172-a-solemn-caution-against-the-ten-h:
Philalethes, lately escaped, wrote A Solemn Caution Against the Ten Horns of Calvinism, fourth edition, Leeds, 1819, as an attack on Calvinist doctrine. Addressing John Wesley, the author tells how, as a youth, he joined the Calvinists, doubted their tenets, and found no peace in books on God's sovereignty. Wesley's Predestination Calmly Considered at last settled his mind.

The ten horns, from Revelation chapter thirteen, stand for ten Calvinist errors the author seeks to expose. His tone is earnest and personal, not academic. The pamphlet shows Methodist argument against predestination in the age of Wesley's followers.
28278-liberalism:
L. T. Hobhouse wrote Liberalism in 1911 for the Home University Library of Modern Knowledge, reprinted many times to 1944. Hobhouse traces liberal ideas from their roots, through civil, fiscal, personal, social, and economic liberty, to Gladstone and Mill, and to the heart of liberalism itself. Chapters treat laissez-faire, the state and the individual, and the future of liberalism.

Hobhouse argues that the modern state, still in the making, grows through a struggle between old and new principles of order. His prose is clear and academic, aimed at general readers. The book remains a classic short statement of British liberal thought.
28339-on-calvinism:
Rev. William Hull, perpetual curate of St. Gregory's, Norwich, wrote On Calvinism in 1841, dedicating it to Dean Pellew. Hull, quoting Eusebius in Greek, argues that God gave humans a natural law and free choice, guiding them to the right path and rewarding the choice of better things. Rivington printed the short treatise in London.

Hull says he does not prejudge the dean's opinion, and takes sole responsibility for his views, free from servile deference. His tone is learned and courteous, aimed at clergy and thoughtful lay readers. The book offers a measured Anglican reply to Calvinist doctrine.
29393-social-justice-without-socialism:
John Bates Clark, professor of political economy at Columbia University, gave these Barbara Weinstock Lectures on the Morals of Trade in 1914, printed by Houghton Mifflin. Clark argues that social justice can be won without socialism, by carrying democracy from politics into social life and by curbing private monopoly in the name of good citizenship. The lectures speak to a Progressive-era audience worried about wealth, power, and fairness.

Clark's case rests on moral economics: fair play in trade, honest dealing, and a state that guards the common good without seizing industry. The prose is plain and earnest, aimed at citizens rather than specialists. Students of American economic thought will find a clear statement of a reform path between laissez-faire and state control.
29881-morals-of-economic-internationalis:
J. A. Hobson gave these Barbara Weinstock lectures on the morals of trade at the University of California, and Houghton Mifflin printed them in 1920. Hobson was known for The Industrial System and The Evolution of Modern Capitalism. The Weinstock series asked scholars and men of affairs to weigh the moral law in business life under the new economic order.

Hobson opens with a plain charge: we hold one moral standard for persons, a slighter one for corporations, and a still slighter one for nations. Corporations, he says, are groupings of persons for personal ends, and nations are wider unions for a common end. Yet the corporation's soul, if it has one, is a leather soul, slow to pity. The lectures press for one standard across all three spheres.
29953-commercialism-and-journalism:
Hamilton Holt, managing editor of The Independent, gave this Barbara Weinstock lecture on the morals of trade, printed in Boston and New York in 1909. The Weinstock series asked scholars and men of affairs to weigh the moral law in business life under the new economic order. Holt's subject is the press itself: commercialism and journalism, and what money does to the moulders of public opinion.

Holt opens with an axiom of old political economy and new sociology alike: public opinion prevails, no law can stand against it, and life is scarcely worth living without its approval. Editors, by common consent, are called the moulders of public opinion, and they love to expatiate on that role over walnuts and wine. Holt presses past the easy talk to the real question of who pays, and what payment costs.
30216-the-buddhist-catechism:
Henry S. Olcott, president-founder of the Theosophical Society, presents Buddhism in question-and-answer form for use in Buddhist schools. High Priest Sumangala of Sripada and the Western Province, principal of Vidyodaya Parivena, approved and recommended the catechism. Olcott dedicates the revised form to his counsellor Hikkaduwe Sumangala at Adyar in 1903. The forty-fourth corrected edition comes from Adyar, London, and Benares in 1915.

Contents move from the life of the Buddha through the Dharma, or doctrine, and the Sangha, to the rise and spread of Buddhism and its relation to science. An appendix gives fourteen propositions accepted by northern and southern Buddhists as a platform of unity. A certificate from Vidyodaya College, Colombo, dated July 7, 1881, stands behind the first edition.
30506-anarchism-and-socialism:
George Plechanoff argues against anarchism and for scientific socialism in a work translated by Eleanor Marx Aveling with the author's permission, published in Chicago by Charles H. Kerr. Nine chapters move from utopian socialists and scientific socialism to the historical growth of anarchist doctrine.

Later chapters study Proudhon and Bakounine at length, then turn to smaller figures, so-called anarchist tactics and their morality, and the bourgeoisie in relation to anarchism and socialism. Plechanoff writes as a Marxist critic, sharp in argument and rich in history. The book serves as a classic statement of the socialist case against anarchist theory and action. His tone is firm, and his case is built on facts, dates, and close reading of rival books.
30538-new-worlds-for-old-a-plain-account:
H. G. Wells writes New Worlds for Old, a plain account of modern socialism, first published in March 1908 and reissued in a popular edition revised in June 1909. The London Constable edition of 1912 lists Wells's stories, romances, novels, and sociological essays, from The Time Machine and The War of the Worlds to Anticipations and A Modern Utopia.

Wells aims to explain socialism in plain terms for ordinary readers, not specialists alone. His introduction opens the case for a new social order, built on shared work, fair distribution, and public purpose. The book serves as an accessible socialist primer from a famous novelist, clear in style and bold in hope.
30545-the-a-b-c-with-the-church-of-engla:
The A, B, C, with the Church of England Catechism, was printed in Philadelphia in 1785 by Young, Stewart, and McCulloch on Chestnut Street. It adds prayers used in the Academy of the Protestant Episcopal Church in Philadelphia. A hymn on the Nativity and another for Easter Day also appear, under the Proverbs text: train up a child in the way he should go.

Roman alphabets, large and small, open the book, followed by italic alphabets and ligatures, giving children letter forms to learn. The catechism and prayers then teach faith in short, memorizable form. The little book serves as an early American primer, blending reading lessons with church teaching for young learners.
30646-woman-under-socialism:
August Bebel writes Woman Under Socialism, translated from the original German of the thirty-third edition by Daniel De Leon and published in New York in 1917 by the Labor News Company. Bebel opens with Bachofen: the end of social development resembles the beginning of human existence, and original equality returns.

A second epigraph argues that property, grown immense and diversified since civilization, has become an unmanageable power, bewildering the mind that created it. Human intelligence, Bebel insists, will rise to mastery over property and define its relations anew. The book argues for women's emancipation through socialism, linking equality, work, and family.
31941-rationalism:
J. M. Robertson's Rationalism, in the Philosophies Ancient and Modern series, stands beside companion volumes on animism, pantheism, and the religions of ancient China and Greece. Others cover Islam, magic and fetishism, and the religions of Egypt, Babylonia, and Assyria. The series presents short, authoritative introductions to philosophies and religions for general readers.

This volume explains rationalism as a way of thinking that tests belief by reason rather than by authority or revelation, and traces its place among ancient and modern philosophies. Readers get a compact introduction to a standpoint that shaped modern science, criticism, and free thought, in a series designed for students and general readers alike.
32252-the-stages-in-the-social-history-o:
Henri Pirenne's The Stages in the Social History of Capitalism is a historical essay offered frankly as a hypothesis. Pirenne writes that he wishes only to develop a hypothesis in the pages that follow, and that readers may find the evidence insufficient. The scarcity of special studies on his subject, at least for the period since the end of the Middle Ages, is enough to discourage more than one cautious spirit, he admits.

Yet Pirenne is convinced that any attempt at synthesis, however early it seems, cannot fail to help investigations, provided it is offered in all frankness for what it is. His ideas received a kind reception at the International Congress of Historical Studies held in London. Readers get a classic historical hypothesis, tracing capitalism's social stages from the Middle Ages onward, modest about its evidence and bold in synthesis.
33214-the-white-queen-of-okoyong-a-true-:
W. P. Livingstone's book tells for young people the true story of Mary Slessor, the White Queen of Okoyong, in Calabar. Copyrighted in 1917, it follows Slessor's life of adventure, heroism, and faith among the peoples of West Africa, from river journeys threatened by wild beasts to her work among villages. Livingstone, who also wrote a longer life of Slessor, shapes the tale for younger readers.

The book's power lies in its plain account of courage and care: a lone woman facing danger, sickness, and strange customs with steady faith. Its scenes, from a canoe attacked by a hippopotamus to quiet acts of mercy, stay vivid. For young readers, it is an inspiring story of a missionary heroine whose life bridged two worlds.
33584-women-as-world-builders-studies-in:
Floyd Dell studies modern feminism through the lives of individual women in this 1913 book. Rather than treat the movement as a sociological abstraction in heavy monographs, Dell follows William James's journalistic method. He takes feminism as the sum of what particular women did, preserving the personal tone and color that give a movement its life.

Eight chapters profile Charlotte Perkins Gilman, Emmeline Pankhurst and Jane Addams, Olive Schreiner and Isadora Duncan, Beatrice Webb and Emma Goldman, Margaret Dreier Robins, Ellen Key, and the Freewomen around Dora Marsden. Dell chose ten representative women to show the soul of modern feminism. The book is a vivid, sympathetic introduction to feminist thought before the First World War.
4095-plato-and-platonism:
Walter Pater's Plato and Platonism reads Plato as a living teacher rather than a museum figure. Pater imagines Plato holding discourses much like his dialogues, only a little better, as a diligent scholar might do on the morrow.

Pythagoras and the Pythagoreans enter the study too, with their wild thought of metempsychosis, the passing of souls, tied to a theory of the visible heaven. Pater weighs Plato's debt to earlier Greek thinkers and his power over later ones. Readers who like philosophy written as fine prose will find a humane, beautiful introduction.
5273-darwiniana-essays-and-reviews-perta:
Asa Gray's Darwiniana, published in New York in 1876, gathers essays and reviews on Darwinism by Harvard's professor of botany. Its first article takes up the Origin of Species, comparing Darwin's views of species with those of Agassiz and the common view. It traces variation, artificial selection, reversion, and natural selection.

Gray, a friend and defender of Darwin who also held religious faith, argued that physical connection of species was compatible with intellectual connection. The book offers readers a contemporary American response to evolution, written by a botanist who knew the science from the inside and welcomed it without surrendering his beliefs.
5624-the-inhumanity-of-socialism:
Edward F. Adams wrote The Inhumanity of Socialism as two papers making the case against socialism. The first was read before the League of the Republic at the University of California on December 5, 1913, and the second before the Ruskin Club of Oakland some years earlier. Adams closes his foreword by urging respect for law, order, the rights of others, admiration for the successful, sympathy with the unfortunate, and charity for all.

The papers argue that socialism offends human nature, law, and ordered liberty. Readers get an early twentieth-century American critique, earnest and polemical, useful for the history of political argument.
5630-the-story-of-mormonism-and-the-phil:
James E. Talmage wrote The Story of Mormonism and The Philosophy of Mormonism from lectures delivered at the University of Michigan, Cornell University, and elsewhere. The Story first appeared as a lecture report in the Improvement Era, then as a booklet, before Talmage revised and reconstructed it for this volume. Chapters treat the Book of Mormon and the faith's origins.

The Philosophy portion sets out Latter-day Saint belief as a system, while the Story narrates its rise. Readers get a clear, sympathetic account by a leading Mormon scholar, useful for anyone seeking the movement's own presentation of its history and ideas.
6302-the-junior-classics-volume-7-storie:
William Patten's seventh Junior Classics volume gathers stories of courage and heroism for boys and girls, introduced by Harvard's Charles W. Eliot. Phidias helps an image maker, Charlotte M. Yonge tells the fight at Thermopylae and the bravery of Regulus, and a rabbi finds a diadem. Livia wins a brooch, Caesar crosses the Rubicon, Saint Genevieve guards Paris, and a boy Viking sails as Olaf of Norway.

Boy heroes of Crecy and Poitiers and the noble burghers of Calais carry the middle of the book. Joan of Arc, maid who saved France, follows, with Catherine Douglas thrusting her arm through staples to save a king. A brave queen of Hungary, Columbus for little children, and a sea fight in Queen Bess's time follow. The volume is an anthology of brave deeds, chosen to give young readers models of steadfast nerve.
6316-poems-of-american-patriotism:
Brander Matthews gathers American patriotic poems, revised and extended, with pictures by N. C. Wyeth and a dedication to Theodore Roosevelt. His prefatory note says the collection holds poems of feeling as well as poems of action, since both show the temper of a time, and most are old favourites. Emerson's Boston, Longfellow's Paul Revere's Ride, and Lanier's Battle of Lexington open the run.

Holmes on Bunker Hill, Pierpont's Warren's address, Finch on Nathan Hale, and Bryant's Song of Marion's Men follow, with Freneau, Lowell on Washington, and Key's Star Spangled Banner. Drake's American Flag, Holmes's Old Ironsides, and O'Hara's Bivouac of the Dead carry the book through later wars. Matthews gives a nation's memory in verse, from Lexington to the bivouac, for readers and classrooms alike.
6320-english-literary-criticism:
C. E. Vaughan sketches how criticism grew in England, and how its methods changed, using one or two typical writers for each phase. He does not try to gather every striking piece, but to show development through samples. Sidney's Apology for Poetry, Dryden's preface to the Fables, and Johnson on the metaphysical poets open the run, with Coleridge, Hazlitt, Lamb, Shelley, Carlyle, and Pater to follow.

Vaughan's introduction calls criticism a late birth, a self conscious art. It could not arise until poets had sung for centuries and readers began to ask what power their work held and by what principles it should be judged. Sidney calls the poet a maker, from the Greek poiein, to make. The anthology, edited with an introduction by Vaughan, is a compact history of English judgment, from defence to theory.
7409-an-essay-on-criticism:
Alexander Pope was twenty-three when he published An Essay on Criticism in 1711, and it made his name. Written in heroic couplets, the poem lays down rules for judging poetry: follow nature, distrust shallow learning, and let wit be nature dressed to advantage. Pope was a Roman Catholic barred from public office, writing from his father's small estate in Windsor Forest, and the poem's polish announced a major talent.

The essay's couplets have entered the language: fools rush in where angels fear to tread, and to err is human, to forgive divine. Beneath the maxims lies a serious argument about taste, pride, and humility before great work. This edition adds introductory and explanatory notes, making Pope's compact, allusive poem open to modern readers.
7421-poems-of-optimism:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox, America's beloved poet of cheer, published Poems of Optimism in 1913, and this edition reprints it in 1919, after the First World War had tested its title. The contents open with war poems: Greater Britain, Belgium, Knitting, Mobilisation, and a book for the king, written while Europe was at war. A peace angel and a plea that peace should not come too cheaply follow.

The optimism of the title is not denial but resolve. Wilcox insists that hearts were not set on fighting, yet swears her people will not yield. The poems mix patriotism with the homely virtues she always praised: courage, kindness, and keeping on. For readers of her famous verse, this is Wilcox facing the hardest years with her faith intact.
7514-a-guide-to-stoicism:
St. George Stock's pocket guide, number 347 in the Ten Cent Pocket Series edited by E. Haldeman-Julius, introduces Stoicism to the general reader. Its foreword strips the philosophy of its paradoxes and wilful misuse of language, and finds what is left: the moral philosophy of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle, dashed with the physics of Heraclitus. Stoicism, Stock argues, was less a new doctrine than the form in which old Greek philosophy presented itself to the world at large.

The guide explains why that form proved popular, owing something to its very extravagance, and what part Stoicism played as a religion and in forming later thought. Conversions between sects were rare, Stock notes, since a choice once made was a man's own and he adhered to it. The book is a clear, short road into a philosophy of endurance.
9912-an-explanation-of-luther-s-small-ca:
Joseph Stump, a Lutheran pastor, wrote this 1910 handbook to help teachers explain Martin Luther's Small Catechism. Luther's short statement of Christian teaching had long been the basic text for young church members, and Stump gives pastors an outline for oral lessons.

Each part is broken down for class use, with a summary pupils could study and review at home. The book walks through the chief parts of the catechism in plain order. It serves readers interested in Lutheran teaching, or in how churches taught the faith to children a century ago.
a-candid-examination-of-theism: George John Romanes examines theism candidly in this essay, first issued under the name Physicus. He asks whether searching can find out God, and weighs the reasons for and against belief. The writer says he held the essay back for years until further thought seemed unlikely to change its conclusions. The result is a frank Victorian inquiry into faith, reason, and evidence.
a-critical-examination-of-socialism: William Hurrell Mallock critically examines socialism as an ostensibly scientific theory. He begins by defining socialism, which he calls an unrealized theory that united many men in a demand for change. The book traces its historical beginning and tests its claims as a system. Mallock argues against socialism with the tools of logic and history.
a-guide-to-stoicism:
St. George Stock, of Pembroke College, Oxford, wrote A Guide to Stoicism as a small handbook, issued in the Ten Cent Pocket Series edited by E. Haldeman-Julius. His foreword strips the subject to a claim: remove the paradoxes and the wilful misuse of language. Stoicism is the moral philosophy of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle, dashed with the physics of Heraclitus.

The guide sketches philosophy among Greeks and Romans, then the Stoic doctrine itself, drawn from the original authorities rather than handbooks. Logic, nature, fate, and the rule of living by reason are set out in short order for a general reader. It aims at the pocket and the railway journey: ancient philosophy made portable without being made shallow.
adventures-in-criticism: Arthur Quiller-Couch gathers essays on reading and writing, opening with Chaucer and moving through poets and prose writers with a critic's sharp eye. He weighs style, taste, and judgment, praising what is vivid and true while faulting what is slack or showy. The pieces mix close reading with lively opinion, offering readers a companionable guide to why some books last and others fade.
an-apology-for-atheism: Charles Southwell writes an apology for atheism, addressed to religious investigators of every denomination by one of its apostles. Published in London, the tract argues the atheist case plainly and boldly for its time. It stands as an early freethought pamphlet, defiant in tone and direct in argument. Its bold stance cost its author dearly in his own day.
an-essay-on-criticism:
Alexander Pope published An Essay on Criticism in 1711, when he was barely into his twenties, and the hosted edition adds a life of the poet plus introductory and explanatory notes. The life recalls his Catholic schooling, his self-teaching after age twelve, and the Twickenham villa from which he became the most popular poet of his age.

The poem itself, in heroic couplets, lays down how to read, judge, and write: follow nature, study the ancients, and distrust pride and petty rules. Famous lines on little learning and on pardoning faults have been quoted ever since. With the notes around it, the edition serves a new reader twice over, giving both the poem and a guided way into Pope's critical world.
an-explanation-of-luther-s-small-catechi: Joseph Stump explains Luther's Small Catechism, opening with Luther's preface from Wittenberg in 1529 and the catechism itself. The explanation walks through the chief parts of Christian teaching as Luther set them out for home and school. It served Lutheran families and classes as a plain guide to the faith. Its plain style suits both home use and class work.
auguste-comte-and-positivism:
John Stuart Mill wrote these essays on Auguste Comte in 1865, judging the French thinker who coined the name Positivism. Mill notes that the phrases Positive Philosophy and Positivism had lately surfaced everywhere, though few knew what they represented. Part one examines Comte's Cours de Philosophie Positive, the great early work of the system.

Praise and warning run together. Mill honours Comte's method and his law-driven view of nature, yet resists the later system built on it. Henry Buckle appears as England's nearest, still distant, parallel: a thinker whose error coloured the doctrine of invariable natural laws with fatalism. The essays remain the sharpest English account of positivism by a philosopher who shared half its ground and fought the other half.
b09-luther-large-catechism:
Martin Luther published the Large Catechism in 1529 for pastors and teachers who had to instruct whole parishes. A catechism teaches faith by question and answer, and Luther's large one treats each part at full length. It covers the Ten Commandments, the Creed, the Lord's Prayer, baptism, and the Lord's Supper.

Luther writes with force and warmth, urging teachers never to think they have learned enough. His preface scolds lazy pastors in terms still quoted today. The book became a fixed standard of Lutheran teaching, kept among its confessional texts. Churches have used it to train clergy ever since. Few teaching books of the age match its plain strength.
b09-luther-small-catechism:
The Small Catechism of 1529 was Martin Luther's handbook for the home, his Enchiridion for heads of households. Where the Large Catechism served pastors, this small one fits in a hand and a memory. It gives the Ten Commandments, the Creed, and the Lord's Prayer in short form.

Baptism, confession, and the Lord's Supper follow, each with brief, clear answers to set questions. Morning and evening prayers and a Table of Duties for each place in life close the book. Luther meant fathers to teach it at table, week by week. It became the most printed Lutheran text after the Bible, and children still learn it today.
britannica-1911-absenteeism:
Absenteeism receives an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The term names landed proprietors who absent themselves from their estates and spend their rents elsewhere. Wider use covers all who draw income from a place while living outside it.

Debate grants the practice a harmful effect, the entry judges. Pre-Revolution France blamed it for poor rural districts, its nobles seldom home unless exiled from Paris. Ireland suffered it as a special evil and taxed it repeatedly: four shillings in the pound in 1727, dropped, restored, reduced, and revived by the Independent Parliament in 1782. Senior, Mill, and McCulloch head the authorities listed. The question mixes wealth drain with moral blame, and the entry leaves both charges standing.
britannica-1911-absolutism:
Absolutism receives an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In aesthetics the word names the theory that beauty is an objective attribute of things, not a mere feeling of pleasure in the perceiver. An absolute standard of the beautiful follows, by which all objects can be judged.

Dissenting connoisseurs are explained by unequal gifts of appreciation, the entry notes. Political philosophy takes the same word for despotic rule, a sovereign unrestrained by laws and based directly on force. Strict cases are rare, it concedes; backward constitutional stages draw the label more loosely. Two fields thus share one term for unconditioned standing, one in the theory of beauty and one in the theory of the state.
britannica-1911-accidentalism:
Accidentalism is a term with three separate lives, and the 1911 Britannica entry keeps them apart. In philosophy it names any system that denies a causal nexus, holding that events follow one another by chance rather than from definite causes. C. S. Peirce called the same view Tychism, from the Greek word for chance, making chance a real factor in the universe.

Ethics borrows the term for the claim that choices are not always caused by motives or character, the liberty of indifference. Painting uses it for effects produced by accidental lights, a usage noted from Ruskin. Medicine uses it for the hypothesis that disease is only an accidental change in a healthy state, avoidable by changing outside conditions.
britannica-1911-achromatism:
Achromatism, in optics, is a simple property. It means passing white light through glass whole. The light is not split into spectrum colours. The 1911 Britannica entry builds the term from Greek. A prefix meaning without joins the word for colour. A lens that keeps white light whole does well. Ordinary lenses fail at exactly that task.

Lenses own the practical point. Achromatic lenses are lenses that have this property. They correct the colour fringing that plagues simple glass. Readers are sent onward for the working detail. The articles on the lens and on aberration hold it. The article on photography holds more. Designers of instruments depend on such lenses. So do photographers who need sharp, true images.
britannica-1911-agnosticism:
Agnosticism is put to the test in the 1911 Britannica by a clash over what counts as knowledge. Men of science deal with facts that can be touched and weighed. They are apt to claim that their laws are final and true in a way no other claims can match. The text that survives here denies that claim. Laws drawn from facts are not the last word, it says. To ask what proof itself rests on is to step past them.

Each side, the piece argues, must grant the other its ground. The man of science trusts what his hands and eyes report. The saint and the theologian trust what they feel in moral and spiritual life. Both rest on a base that can not be proved to one who denies it. Cited books close the entry. They include Stephen's Agnostic's Apology and Flint's Agnosticism.
britannica-1911-algae-polymorphism:
Polymorphism, a section of the Algae article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, treats the many forms a single alga may take. Tracing algal relationships is hard because so few species have been followed from spore to spore. Of thousands of named kinds, most are known only from slices of their life-cycle. Their watery home and minute size hide the missing stages.

Observers long classified algae by their reproductive organs, assuming those show the plant at its most characteristic stage. The risk is plain: stages may escape notice entirely, and plants named as separate kinds may be one life in two shapes. Cases such as Botrydium and Protosiphon, drawn into each other's life-cycles by different authors, show the tangle. Klebs insists that only exact knowledge of each form's conditions can settle whether two named algae are truly distinct or phases of one.
britannica-1911-animism:
Animism is the doctrine of spiritual beings. E. B. Tylor supplied that classic definition. The term derives from anima, meaning soul. Human souls fall within the doctrine. Practice often extends the term further. Animatism attributes mind to inanimate things. Rivers and stones gain reason and will. The entry insists on separating these ideas. Confusing them muddles the whole subject.

Practice makes the distinction hard, though. No people lacks some animistic philosophy. Theory suggests animatism came first historically. Savage thought is no more consistent than civilised thought. One person may hold both doctrines together. Different nature explanations may differ in origin. The long article traces souls, ghosts, and nature spirits. Spencer's sociology and folklore journals anchor the references. Stahl's vital principle appears for the philosophical side.
britannica-1911-archaism: Archaism is an old-fashioned usage in language. The adjective form is archaic. The word comes from a Greek term meaning old. An archaism may survive from earlier speech unintentionally. Writers also employ archaisms deliberately. That deliberate use adopts out-of-date expression for effect. An ancient mode of speaking is the result. The entry is a brief dictionary-style definition, giving the term's Greek origin and its two shades of meaning.
britannica-1911-automatism:
Automatism is a philosophical term with two main senses. In ethics it means man is not responsible. His actions then have no moral value. In psychology it covers actions without conscious endeavour. Conation, or striving, is absent from them. Descartes held all animal action mechanical. Lower animals were pure machines for him. Later thinkers applied that theory to man.

A difference marks the human application, though. Consciousness accompanies mechanical action in man. It is entirely disconnected from it causally. Brain changes result in a given action. Mental desire does not cause that change. Huxley maintained this theory prominently. Hodgson maintained it as well. Psychophysical parallelism must be distinguished from it. That rival theory posits a single mind-stuff. Both mental and physical phenomena result from it. Automatic acts divide into two kinds in conclusion.
britannica-1911-automorphism: Automorphism is a term for reading other people through oneself. Built from the Greek autos, self, and morphē, form, it names the conception and interpretation of other people's habits and ideas on the analogy of one's own. The entry is a single-sentence definition only: the habit of assuming that others think, feel, and act as one does oneself, explained through the word's Greek parts.
britannica-1911-bimetallism:
Bimetallism is a money system in which gold and silver both serve as currency. The 1911 Britannica article gives the term a strict sense. Both metals must be freely received by the mint. Both must pass as full legal tender at a fixed legal ratio. One ounce of gold, for example, might equal a set weight of silver. Where two metals merely circulate side by side at market rates, the article calls that unrated bimetallism instead.

H. Cernuschi coined the word in 1869 for an international plan. Several states would adopt one shared ratio between the metals. The article weighs the theory for and against at great length. It covers price swings, mint behaviour, and the strain a wrong ratio puts on trade. A long book list ends the piece, split by side. Bimetallic League works face Giffen's Case against Bimetallism and Farrer's gold-standard papers.
britannica-1911-buddhism:
Buddhism is the religion of the followers of the Buddha. It covers a large area of India and Asia. This long 1911 Britannica article sets out its doctrines and history. It begins with the Buddha's first discourse. He preached it to the five men he first tried to win. The text survives in the sacred books, in two places. The entry takes it as the best summary of his teaching.

That sermon rejects two opposite aims in life. One is devotion to pleasure and the passions. The other, by contrast, is self-torment. The article follows the discourse into the core doctrines. It then traces the order the Buddha founded. It covers the spread of the faith across Asia. Later schools and their differences also get treatment. The entry gives the reader a full map of the religion. It rests throughout on the oldest documents it can cite.
britannica-1911-cartesianism:
Cartesianism is a long 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on the philosophy developed chiefly in the works of Descartes, Malebranche, and Spinoza. The entry argues that the three men must be read together, since one and the same thought rules them all at different stages of its growth. Malebranche came prepared by Augustine and Spinoza by Jewish philosophy, yet the entry holds that neither bent the system off its own course.

On this view, the later thinkers only drew out consequences that lay inside Descartes's principles from the start. Malebranche appears as the system's interpreter, bold in speculation but held back by the traditions of the Catholic church. Spinoza stands apart, more fully cut off from the religious and secular world of his time than any monk. The entry thus treats Cartesianism as a single unfolding argument rather than three separate philosophies, and follows its inner logic through each man's work.
britannica-1911-chauvinism:
Chauvinism is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a term for unreasonable and exaggerated patriotism. The entry calls it the French equivalent of “Jingoism.” The word did not start there. It originally signified idolatry of Napoleon. It was taken from a much wounded veteran, Nicholas Chauvin. By his adoration of the emperor, Chauvin became the type of blind enthusiasm for national military glory.

That is the whole of the short entry. It defines the term by its excess: patriotism pushed past reason. It then anchors the word in one man's fame. A single soldier's devotion to Napoleon, repeated as a byword, gave French and then English a name for the vice. Readers get a definition, an English parallel, and an origin story in three sentences. The entry trusts the name Chauvin to carry the rest of the meaning.
britannica-1911-chiliasm: Chiliasm, from a Greek word built on chilioi, a thousand, is the belief that Christ will return to reign in the body for a thousand years. The entry gives that doctrine its other name, the Millennium. It sends readers to the article under that head for fuller treatment. No teachers, dates, texts or branches of the belief are named here. The entry stands as a short definition of a single religious idea, fixing its term, its Greek root and its core claim.
britannica-1911-creatianism-and-traducia:
Creatianism and traducianism are two rival doctrines on the origin of the human soul. Traducianism, taught by Tertullian in his De anima, holds that souls are generated from souls as bodies are from bodies. Creatianism holds that God creates a fresh soul for each body that is generated. The names grew from the Latin tradux, a word tied to a figure of speech in Tertullian's text.

Augustine never settled the question, though Pelagians had linked traducianism with the doctrine of original sin. Jerome condemned traducianism and called creatianism the view of the Church. Creatianism later became the general view of medieval theologians, and Peter Lombard gave it a set formula. Luther stayed undecided, but Lutherans mostly held traducianism, while Calvin favoured creatianism. The entry closes by noting that modern thought still leaves the origin of the soul open.
britannica-1911-criticism:
Criticism, from Greek words for a judge and for deciding, is the art of judging the worth of works in literature and the fine arts. Matthew Arnold called it a disinterested effort to learn and spread the best that is known and thought. The entry insists that criticism does not mean fault-finding. A flawless work is as fit a subject for it as a poor one.

A critic, then, is a judge of literary and artistic merit, bound to judge without favour or bias. The long entry that follows traces the history of that art across the ages. Its closing lists name the classic guides, from Aristotle's Poetics in Butcher's edition to Longinus on the Sublime. Modern masters named include Sainte-Beuve, Matthew Arnold, Brunetière, Anatole France, and Walter Pater. The history and the reading list together map how judging art became a literature of its own.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adoptionism:
Adoptionism is a christological theory holding Christ as man God's adoptive Son, though its precise import varies by stage. Roughly there are three forms. First, Elipandus and Felix's eighth-century Adoptionism. Second, Abelard's twelfth-century Neo-Adoptionism. Third, the qualified Adoptionism of later theologians.

The original form asserts Christ's double sonship: one by generation and nature, and one by adoption and grace. As God, Christ is Son by generation and nature, but as man he is Son only by adoption and grace. Elipandus, Archbishop of Toledo under Mohammedan rule, and Felix, Bishop of Urgel under Frankish dominion, held this theory late in the eighth century. Its origin is obscure. Nestorianism was an Eastern heresy, yet an offshoot appeared in the far west, where a Nestorian colony had found refuge in Islamic Spain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agnosticism:
Agnosticism is a philosophical theory of knowledge's limits, professing doubt or disbelief about what the mind can know, in part or whole. The word Agnostic, from Greek a, privative, plus gnostikos, knowing, comes from Professor Huxley in 1869. It described one who saw all attempts to know the reality behind ultimate scientific, philosophic, and religious ideas as futile.

Huxley contrasted his own unpretentious ignorance with the vain knowledge claimed by second- and third-century Gnostics. That antithesis, the entry argues, was unfair and overdrawn, serving to discredit natural theology by classing it with Gnostic vapourings. Rather, Gnostic and Agnostic are the real extremists. The former stretches knowledge's bounds unduly, the latter narrows them. Natural theology, or theism, holds the middle ground between claiming the mind can know everything and claiming it can know nothing about religious truth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agrarianism:
Agrarianism takes its name from Latin agrarius, applied historically to laws or their supporters favouring division of Roman public lands among poorer citizens. So agrarianism and agrarian in English generally imply theories and movements meant to benefit poorer classes by dealing somehow with land ownership or farmers' legal duties. In German, Agrar means rural, and the Agrarpartei matches England's former country party.

Keeping to the stricter use, two social movements running through history stand out: agrarian reform and agrarian revolution. Conspicuous among reforms is the Hebrew Prophets' case. How far the Mosaic Law's land system ever fully worked is disputed, probably unascertainable; ascertainable is the growth, alongside wealth and commerce under the kings, of Hebrew peasantry ill-treatment. Over-taxation for a luxurious court, corn-jobbery and monopoly, and usurious loans made the peasant a debtor-slave or dispossessed him entirely.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alcoholism:
Alcoholism, as this entry uses the term, covers every change alcohol can bring about in the human body. These range from brief exhilaration to deep unconsciousness, coma, and even death. The effects vary with the amount taken, the form of alcohol, how fast it is given, and how used the person is to it. Alcohol itself is about ninety-one per cent ethyl alcohol by weight and nine per cent water.

The entry follows alcohol through the body. All vital processes play out inside the cell., and nearly all alcohol taken passes from the stomach into the blood and straight to the liver by the portal vein. It then considers the effects on organs and tissues, including the skin, where alcohol excites a sense of heat. Physiologists agree on the facts of alcohol's action, the entry notes, but differ sharply on the conclusions to draw from them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altruism:
Altruism is a term Auguste Comte formed in 1851 from the Italian altrui, for benevolent as against selfish propensities. George H. Lewes brought it into English in 1853, and Comte's expounders popularized it. Psychologically it names reflective emotions benefiting others, but its important sense is ethical.

Comte's religious system won few adherents, too extravagant even for Littré, one of his earliest able followers. Catholic teaching sums love of others in Christ's precept, love thy neighbour as thyself, with self-love as exemplar but not measure. Catholic ethics reconciles self-love and benevolence under creation's supreme purpose, allowing self-love moral quality and subordinating both to the Creator's ends.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anglicanism:
Anglicanism denotes the belief and position of the established Church of England and communicating churches in British lands, the United States, and elsewhere. It includes those who accepted the English Reformation as embodied in the Church of England or in offshoot churches adhering to its doctrines and liturgy. Apart from minor settlements, its area matches lands under the British flag.

The article sketches Anglicanism in the Established Church in three periods. Henry VIII's reign was ostensibly conservative, aiming at a Catholic Church minus the pope, yet his actions contradicted him. The Edwardian and Elizabethan periods carried separation further. In belief, Anglicans accept Scripture as containing all things necessary to salvation, take the Prayer Book as the rule of worship, and recognize Baptism and the Lord's Supper. The clergy subscribe the Thirty-nine Articles. Three schools divide Anglican thought: Low, Broad, and High Church, culminating in the Oxford Movement of 1833.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-animism:
Animism, from Latin anima, soul, is the theory of the soul. In current language it has a twofold meaning. Philosophically, it holds the soul to be life's principle in man and other living things. For man, it embodies spiritualistic philosophy as opposed to materialistic philosophy. Animism seeks knowledge of man's nature, establishing the soul's existence, nature, union with the body, origin, and duration. These problems underlie conscious existence and mental and moral studies.

Ethnologically, it is a recent theory of religion's origin, the ghost theory. At bottom it is a biological theory, explaining phenomena by living analogy. To primitive man, all moving things lived, and ghost fancy soon extended to all objects. Spiritual beings are modelled on man's own soul. Burial customs illustrate it: horses and camels slain at graves, food and weapons in tombs, surviving in paper messengers burned and substitutes on graves in China and Japan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anthropomorph:
Anthropomorphism, from anthropos, man, and morphe, form, means man pictures the outer world's acts as his own. A system built on this bent is called philosophic. But most often it means that bent at work in faith. In faith, it gives the Supreme Being human form, limbs, operations, and traits.

This bent shows strongly in primitive heathen faiths and in all polytheism, especially in Greek and Roman pagan worship. Xenophanes of Colophon charged the Greeks with it. The first Christian apologists blamed pagans for showing God in human form. Throughout the Fathers, God's spirituality, and man's weak grasp of His boundless perfection, are stressed again and again. Yet Catholic philosophy forms its idea of God from our own minds and moral characteristics, while noting all made good falls far short of God's own good.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antinomianism:
Antinomianism, anti, against, and nomos, law, holds Christians free from moral law. The term arose in Luther's day for Agricola's teachings. Pushing faith-alone to a logical conclusion, Agricola held good works do not promote salvation, nor evil works hinder it. Justified Christians, he held, cannot lose holiness or their saved state by disobedience or violation of God's law.

After doubtful standing among slanderers warned against by the Apostle, Antinomianism came back as a variant of Protestant faith doctrine early in the German Reformation. It set Luther and his disciple and fellow townsman Agricola, born at Eisleben in 1492, at odds. The doctrine is mostly held in theory, seldom urged in practice, and was banned by the Council of Trent's decree on Justification, whose fifteenth chapter concerns this heresy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apollinariani:
Apollinarianism is a Christological theory, a teaching about the nature of Christ. It holds that he had a human body and a human feeling soul, but no human rational mind, with the divine Logos, or Word, taking the mind's place. Its author, Apollinaris the Younger, bishop of Laodicea, was active in the later fourth century. He was first highly esteemed by Athanasius, Basil, and Jerome for learning, biblical knowledge, and loyalty to the Nicene faith.

With his father, Apollinaris the Elder, he recast Scripture on classical models to make up for Greek literature lost when Julian's edict barred Christians from teaching it. Jerome credits him with countless volumes on Scripture, two defences of Christianity, and a refutation of Eunomius, but those works are lost. Surviving tracts on his theory, some circulated under false names, let readers see how the church answered a teaching that denied Christ a full human mind.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arianism:
Arianism, a heresy that arose in the fourth century and rejected the divinity of Jesus Christ, ranks first among disputes that troubled Christians after Constantine recognized the church in 313. It fathered many more over three centuries. It will seem strange to modern eyes, since it is not modern unbelief but an eastern attempt to rationalize the creed.

In the New Testament and church teaching Jesus appears as Son of God, a name he took to himself. John's gospel calls him the Word, or Logos, who existed with God from the beginning and was God, maker of all things. Paul's genuine letters to Ephesians, Colossians, and Philippians lay down a like doctrine. Arianism, denying that full divinity, forced the church to define what it meant by Son and Word, and the entry follows that long definition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arminianism:
Arminianism is the popular name for doctrines held by a party formed early in the seventeenth century among Calvinists of the Netherlands. Human reason, the article argues, revolted against Calvin's horrible decree of absolute predestination. Salvation and damnation were dealt out without regard to merit, and opposition stirred from the dogma's first promulgation. While religious wars gripped the masses, thoughtful minds were few and uninfluential, and Calvin's tenets, the article charges, banished charity and mercy and bred strife and bloodshed.

Calm deliberation could not sustain that spirit, and a leader was sure to rise from Calvinist ranks to expose the Genevan creed's harmful corollaries. That leader was Jacobus Arminius, born Jakob Hermanzoon at Oudewater and professor at Leyden University. The entry follows his teaching, its clash with strict Calvinism, and the party that took his name into the churches of Holland and beyond.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-asceticism:
Asceticism comes from Greek askesis, meaning practice, bodily exercise, and above all athletic training. Early Christians adopted it for the practice of spiritual things, or spiritual exercises performed to gain habits of virtue. Today it is often used scornfully for religious practices of eastern fanatics as well as Christian saints, lumped together by some. It is often confused with austerity, even by Catholics, but wrongly, the article argues.

Though flesh lusts against spirit and repression and self-denial are needed to control animal passions, virtue cannot be measured by the extent of bodily penances. External penances even in saints are viewed with suspicion. Jerome, prone to austerity himself and therefore a valuable witness, is cited on that caution. The long article separates disciplined training from mere harshness, tracing ascetic practice through scripture, fathers, and saints.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-atavism:
Atavism, from Latin atavus, a great-grandfather's grandfather or ancestor, is a term Duchesne introduced for cases where species revert spontaneously to presumably long-lost characters. Most authors use atavism and reversion in the same sense. The term expresses the reappearance, in individual or race, of physical or psychical traits supposed once held by remote ancestors.

Very often such reappearing traits are monstrous, for example the three-toed horse, whose condition is read as harking back to Tertiary times, when the modern horse's ancestor held three toes. The use of the term in teratology, the study of monstrosities, is often abused, the article warns. Many so-called atavistic monstrosities bear little relation to lost characters, such as extra human digits. The entry separates genuine reversion from loose labelling.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-atheism:
Atheism, from a privative and theos, God, meaning without God, is the system of thought formally opposed to theism, belief in God. Since first use the term has been employed very vaguely, generally as an accusation against any system questioning the popular gods of the day. Socrates was accused of atheism, Diagoras was called atheist by Cicero, and Democritus and Epicurus were styled impious, without respect for gods, for their new atomistic philosophy.

In the same sense early Christians were known to pagans as atheists because they denied heathen gods, and various religious and philosophical systems have likewise been deemed atheistic. Historically, atheism has often meant no more than critical or sceptical rejection of the theology of those using the term as a charge. The long article moves from that loose label to formal atheism as a system, its arguments, and the Catholic reply.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-atomism:
Atomism holds that every body is built from minute, indivisible particles called atoms. Leucippus began the philosophy, and his pupil Democritus, born about 460 BC, gave it its classic shape. For Democritus, atoms are eternal and countless, and differences among things come from their size, shape, and place. Epicurus added a slight swerve to falling atoms, and Lucretius defended the theory in verse.

After a long gap, Gassendi revived Epicurean atomism in the 1600s and tried to fit it with Christian belief. The entry then weighs the scientific form against scholastic critics, who read chemical change as a deep change of substance. For those critics, a formula shows how elements react, not a building made of fixed atoms. It ends by calling broad claims about radioactivity premature, since the science of the day could not yet settle the question.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baptism:
Baptism is one of the Church's seven sacraments, often called the first sacrament and the door of the Church. The entry treats it under many heads, from doctrine and etymology to matter, form, minister, and ceremonies. It opens with two authoritative documents, chiefly Eugene IV's Decree for the Armenians in the bull Exultate Deo. That decree calls baptism the door of spiritual life, making us members of Christ and of the Church.

Substitutes, rebaptism, unbaptized infants, and the sacrament's effects are also treated. Closing sections treat metaphorical baptisms, such as the blessing of bells and of ships. Bells, washed with holy water and anointed inside and out, are blessed to rout demons, guard against storms, and call prayer. Ships have been blessed since Crusader times, recalling Noah's ark and Peter sinking in the sea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benthamism:
Benthamism, the philosophy of Jeremy Bentham, receives a critical entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Bentham, an English jurist born in London in 1748, left the bar in disgust at legal chicanery and spent his life rethinking law. Locke, Hume, Montesquieu, and Beccaria shaped his turn to the principles of legislation.

His test was utility: the greatest happiness of the greatest number, judged by pleasures and pains. The entry follows that test through law, punishment, and government, then weighs it against Catholic moral teaching. It finds the calculus clever but thin on duty, rights, and the higher goods of human life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-biblical-crit:
Biblical criticism in its textual sense, the recovery of a lost original text, receives a very long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. It differs from higher criticism, which studies sources, date, and influence. Textual work applies only where the author's own manuscript is gone, since a surviving autograph could simply be photographed or reprinted.

No two hand copies of a long work ever agree in every detail, as the Augsburg Confession of 1530 shows: thirty-five copies made within months already differ, and its originals are lost. The entry explains collation, manuscripts, and versions as the tools for rebuilding the Bible's text as closely as scholarship allows.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-birds-in-symb:
Birds in symbolism, the Christian meanings given to birds, receive a charming entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. The dove leads, standing for the Holy Spirit, who descended like a dove at Jesus's baptism, and for peace, since a dove brought Noah an olive branch when the flood ended. Early art painted apostles and faithful as doves.

Other birds follow, each with a moral: the eagle for renewal and lofty sight, the pelican for self-giving love, the phoenix for resurrection. The entry gathers Scripture, art, and bestiary lore into a small aviary of faith. It shows how the Church read nature as a picture book.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brahminism:
Brahminism, the religion and social system grown from Aryan nature worship in northern India, survives in its modern form as Hinduism. Its earliest sacred books, first spoken then written between 1500 and 400 before Christ, begin with four Vedas. They hold hymns of the Rig-Veda, the Sama-Veda's song-service, the Yajur-Veda's liturgy, and the Atharva-Veda's spells and charms.

Brahmanas explain Vedic rites, Upanishads ponder deity and man's end, and Sutras guide daily rites and law, crowned by the Laws of Manu. Later sections trace early Vedism's many nature gods, popular worship, pantheistic thought, early and sectarian Hinduism, and reform movements. The entry thus maps a faith from simple polytheism to a vast, intricate system still alive today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-buddhism:
Buddhism, a religious and monastic system founded about 500 before Christ, grew from pantheistic Brahminism through the Vedanta school's search for release. Vedanta thinkers shared a gloomy view that conscious life is a burden, with happiness only in dreamless, desire-free sleep, and they accepted rebirth's endless chain. Breaking with Vedic rites, they sought escape from rebirth and conscious being, and Buddhism won the greatest fame among these rival paths.

Its founder, Gotama, son of a petty raja on Nepal's southern border, learned the Vedas, married young, and kept a prince's household before worldly pleasures palled. He left home for forest austerity, nearly died of fasting, and turned to long meditation, believing he had found the sole path from rebirth's misery to Nirvana. Preaching first at Benares, his earnest eloquence won warriors and Brahmins alike to his gospel of deliverance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-calvinism:
Calvinism takes its shape from Calvin's Institutes of the Christian Religion, never replaced by any creed, though Calvin signed the Augsburg Confession at Worms in 1540. Coming after Luther, he fought Zwingli's followers at Zurich, who leaned toward a Christianity without mysteries. In 1549 he joined Bullinger in the Consensus of Zurich, a middle view of the Eucharist. A compact of Geneva's pastors in 1552 backed him against Jerome Bolsec on predestination; he refuted Bolsec and jailed him.

Later Eucharist disputes drew Calvin toward Melanchthon's party. Beza softened Geneva's doctrine toward the Lutherans, and the many creeds faded as the Institutes stood as the sum of Reformed theology. Three currents have run through this Protestant growth ever since: mystic from Wittenberg, logical and orthodox from Geneva, and heterodox and rationalist from Zurich. In church life each member must sign formulas, submit to discipline, and be ruled by elders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chrism:
An entry on chrism, the mixture of olive oil and balsam blessed by a bishop and used in sacraments and sacred functions. For Confirmation to be valid, the chrism must be pure olive oil blessed by a bishop, or by a priest deputed by the Holy See. Probably it should also contain balsam and receive a blessing distinct from those of the oil of the sick and the oil of catechumens. If those last conditions fail, the sacrament stands doubtfully valid.
