Chrism first meant any smearing stuff, but the Fathers narrowed it to the sacred oil of Baptism and Confirmation. Origen speaks of the visible chrism of baptism, and Cyril of Jerusalem praises the mystic chrism. Early councils treat it as set apart for sanctifying men.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-collectivism:
John Augustine Ryan's entry defines collectivism as a later and more precise term than socialism. Socialism is often used loosely, even for single-tax plans or state ownership of railways and telegraphs. Collectivism is scarcely used except for one system. In it, the public owns and manages the material means of production. It usually marks only the economic side of socialism. It carries no set philosophy, psychology, ethics, or history of its own.

Ryan allows wide variety in how the system might work. He notes that many old arguments against it have lost force as its theory grew clearer. The entry closes near official Catholic teaching. A pope declared that human welfare demands private ownership of stable possessions and of lucrative property, a limit that pure economic collectivism must face.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-communism:
John Augustine Ryan's entry defines communism in a broad and a strict sense. Broadly it covers any system where the group owns all property, or at least all productive property, instead of individuals. That sweep takes in communistic anarchism, socialism, and strict communism. Anarchists of this school would end both private property and government. Socialism claims only the material means of production. Strict communism claims consumption goods too: dwellings, furniture, food, and clothing, all held by the whole community.

History opens with Crete near 1300 B.C., then the first Christians of Jerusalem, then medieval heretical sects. French writers of the eighteenth century rebuilt society in theory, and Cabet's Voyage en Icarie of 1840 followed More's model. American experiments fill the later pages: Ephrata, the Shakers, the Harmonists of 1805, the Separatists of Zoar, Oneida, some thirty Fourierist phalanxes of the 1840s, and the Amana community of 1855.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-confucianism:
Charles Francis Aiken's entry defines Confucianism as the moral, social, political, and religious system Confucius built on ancient Chinese tradition, kept as state religion. It aims to form the virtuous, learned man of good manners. The perfect man joins saint, scholar, and gentleman. It is a religion without positive revelation, with minimal dogma. Popular worship centers on offerings to the dead. Duty stretches beyond morals into daily life's details.

Confucius, K'ung-tze or K'ung-fu-tze, latinized by Jesuit missionaries, was born in 551 B.C. in a feudal state. Aiken treats teacher, texts, and doctrine in turn. Texts include History, Songs, Changes, Rites with the Doctrine of the Mean and Great Learning, and Mencius. Jesuit researches first opened these books to the West. Aiken closes contrasting Confucian rites, polygamy, and seclusion of women with Christian civilization.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregationa:
James Loughlin's entry traces Congregationalism from Anglican bishops' rule and Catholic rites that offended Protestants, which bred many Puritan factions of varying radicalism. Elizabeth and the Stuarts enforced conformity by force. Timid Puritans stayed in the State Church, protesting popish leanings to the present day. Advanced leaders saw no place in a church ruled by bishops and tied to civil power. Geneva seemed Christ's kingdom on earth, and Scotland drew them toward Presbyterian-style churches.

Many then pressed further, forming independent churches on congregational lines. New England colonies proved decisive for the movement, whose American Puritans preferred the term Congregationalism. Its order holds that the elect, called one by one by the Lord through word and Spirit, walk together in particular societies or churches. Doctrine stayed mostly strict Calvinist. Churches thrived best under persecution's glue; once it lifted, loose order left them open. Congregational unions later answered that weakness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congruism:
Walter McDonald's entry defines Congruism, theologians' term for a theory on efficacious grace. Efficacy owes, at least in part, to grace given in favorable circumstances, hence congruous. Augustine already distinguished gratia congrua from gratia incongrua, calling the elect congruenter vocati in his reply to Simplicianus, book one, question two. Jesuit theologians developed the system at the close of the sixteenth century and the start of the seventeenth.

All Molinists identify actual grace with supernatural action. Actual grace of will, technically inspiration, is an act of will. It begins necessarily and may become free at a point in its duration. The live question follows: why, of two motions similar in constitution, does one prove efficacious and the other not? Motives sway the will, and Molinists hold that before grace, sufficient or efficacious, God knows by scientia media whether it will result. Billuart and other opponents of Molinism pressed the contrary reading.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-creationism:
This doctrinal entry sorts out three meanings of creationism. In the widest sense it is the doctrine that God made the material of the universe from no prior subject, against all forms of pantheism. Less widely, it holds that living species were directly created by God, not produced by evolution. In its restricted and usual sense, it concerns the human soul alone.

That third sense is the entry's real subject. It argues that the soul, being spiritual and indivisible, cannot come from parents by generation or emanate from God. It must be immediately created by God. The entry weighs rival views, including Traducianism, and notes which questions theologians still leave open.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-deism:
A long entry defines deism as the tendency of thought and criticism that appeared chiefly in England late in the seventeenth century, though French, German, pagan, Jewish, and Muslim deists also existed. Its writers, often called freethinkers, cast off authoritative religious teaching for free rational speculation, and cannot be grouped as one school or one system.

Many were frankly materialistic, and French thinkers building on English deism were almost wholly so. Others kept a religion of nature. The entry sketches the leading English writers in turn: Herbert of Cherbury, Blount, Toland, Shaftesbury, Collins, Woolston, Tindal, Morgan, Chubb, Bolingbroke, Annet, and Dodwell. Each receives his doctrines, methods, and chief works, showing a movement united less by positive teaching than by critical attitude toward revelation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-determinism:
A philosophy entry on determinism, the theory, named widely since Mill, that every act of will is fixed by earlier conditions. It stands against free will in two main forms. Biological and materialistic versions trace each choice to the body's physical state, while psychological versions trace it to character joined with the motives pressing at the moment.

Supporters reject the labels of necessarianism and fatalism, which hint at outside compulsion, and stress only steady sequence between motive and choice. Opponents answer that the self itself causes volition, freely and from within. If determinism held, the entry argues, responsibility, merit, sin, and reward would turn illusory, and ethics itself would fall.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-druidism:
Druidism takes its name, by a favorite guess since Pliny, from the Greek word for oak, making druids priests of the oak god. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that the oak looms large in Aryan cult, and the Welsh word for druid, derwydd, seems to back the guess. Yet the Irish draoi resists easy matching, and the best-grounded derivation traces druid to a root for knowing, with an intensive prefix, giving the very wise and learned ones.

Even that reading is only conjecture, and the word and the institution may not be Celtic at all. The entry surveys what can be known of druid priests, their learning, and their rites, drawing on Anwyl, Bertrand, and Dottin. It leaves the reader with a mystery framed by the best guesses of scholarship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dualism:
Dualism, from the Latin for two, is a name used by different schools in different senses. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry starts with the religious sense, a system that explains the world as the clash of two eternal opposed principles, good and evil, light and darkness. The theory ran widely through the East, above all in Persia for centuries before Christ. The Zend-Avesta, ascribed to Zoroaster of the sixth century before Christ, sets the world as a struggle between Ormuzd and Ahriman.

Ormuzd is infinite light, supreme wisdom, and author of all good, while Ahriman is the prince of darkness and evil. The entry then turns to philosophical dualism and to the writers who fought natural dualism, from Berkeley to Bradley. It offers a map of a word that has meant war in heaven and division in the mind.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dynamism:
Dynamism names a family of views about what matter is. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes their shared ground amid all their differences: matter consists of simple, indivisible units, substances, or forces. Some systems admit matter and extension with intrinsic tendencies and forces, but dynamism proper goes further. It dissolves the matter-force dualism by turning matter itself into force.

The entry limits itself to this strict form, first naming its chief advocates and characteristic shapes, then comparing them for points of likeness and difference. It closes with modern physicists such as Rutherford, Lodge, and Thomson, and with popular works on the electrical nature of matter. For students of philosophy, it maps a theory that dissolves solidity into energy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eastern-monas:
In Egypt's desert, where men fled persecution and the peril of apostasy to serve God alone, Eastern monasticism began. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry counts Saint Anthony, who lived from 270 to 356, as father of all monks. His fame drew crowds, so that under Diocletian and Constantine large colonies of monks filled Egypt, the first laurae. Saint Athanasius, sheltered by them in his exiles, spread their fame.

The monks dwelt each in his own hut, working with their hands and obeying an elder hermit, meeting for common prayer on Saturday and Sunday. The entry follows the life from Egypt to the Byzantine world and to Eastern Catholic monasteries of today, among them Grottaferrata outside Rome. Eastern bishops, it notes, are not always monks, since many unmarried secular priests serve.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eastern-schis:
Most Eastern Christians were cut from union with the Catholic Church by the great quarrel known as the Eastern Schism. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry warns against picturing it as one sudden break after centuries of peace. Schisms ran through the East from the days of Diotrephes, and Arian, Nestorian, and Monophysite breaks still last. The Eastern Schism means the final parting that made the separated Orthodox Church.

Its remote preparation stretched over centuries of drift, rivalry, and misunderstanding, not one dispute alone. The entry points readers to Photius, Michael Caerularius, and the Council of Florence for the details. It closes by calling the schism not only the greatest but also the most needless evil in Christendom, a wound both sides might yet heal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eclecticism:
Eclecticism, from Greek words for choosing out, means either a thinker's bent to reconcile rival views. It can also mean a system that solves problems by picking and joining what it counts true in each school. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that, in the first sense, eclecticism marks all great philosophers, with special growth in Leibniz, as one strand of the integral method of philosophy. The name eclectics, however, fits those who take eclecticism as the true and basic system.

It is with eclecticism in that strict sense that the entry deals. In philosophy's history, eclecticism as a rule comes after ages of system building, gathering the schools' harvest. The entry cites Cousin, Leroux, Taine, and Mercier, giving readers both the habit of mind and the school that bears its name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-egoism:
Egoism is the name for moral systems that make self-love the root of right action. In a wide sense any system that puts some good of the self first could count. Usage gives the name to systems that make happiness, pleasure, or personal gain the sole end of conduct. The idea runs through the Cyrenaic, Epicurean, Utilitarian, and Evolutionary schools.

Its clearest voices are Hobbes and Mandeville. Bentham states it in full: pleasure alone is good, pain alone is evil, and every motive is the chase of pleasure or the flight from pain. The entry presses the hard case against it, namely kindly acts done for no gain. Hobbes turns such acts into hidden hopes and fears, and later writers say virtue first sought for pleasure comes in time to be sought for itself. It also notes that pleasures and pains resist exact measuring.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-emanationism:
Emanationism is the doctrine that all things flow forth from a First Reality, and this entry sets out its shape with care. The word itself is a metaphor, used in many senses and often by writers who are not emanationists at all. Taken as commonly received, it answers not what God is, but how things come from God. Each being flows from the one before it, in a series that starts with God.

At every step the derived being is less perfect than its source, yet the source loses nothing by giving rise to others. The first source stays unchanged, neither used up nor lessened. Emanationism is often called a form of pantheism. The entry draws a line. Pantheism identifies all things with one substance, while emanationism concerns the mode of derivation. Many emanationists deny that derived things share the source's substance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-embolism:
Embolism means an insertion, and in church language it has two quite different uses, both explained here. In the Mass it is the prayer set between the Our Father and the breaking of the bread, beginning Libera nos, quaesumus, Domine, deliver us, Lord, from all evils. It unfolds the last petition of the Our Father, and in varied forms it appears in nearly all Western liturgies and many Eastern ones.

The Roman form adds a plea for peace naming Mary, Peter, Paul, and Andrew, whose name already stands in the Gelasian Sacramentary. In the calendar, embolism means the gap between the lunar year of three hundred and fifty-four days and the solar year. In the nineteen-year Alexandrian cycle seven extra months were added, making seven years of thirteen lunar months, called embolistic years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-empiricism:
Empiricism is the theory that knowledge comes only from experience, and this entry traces it in psychology and in logic. In psychology it says the facts of consciousness are simply the product of sense experience, of sensations joined and arranged, and it stands against nativism, or innatism. In logic it says all human knowledge springs solely from experience: sense perceptions from outside, plus inner pictures and inferences, with no immaterial factor of mind at work.

It thus opposes intellectualism, rationalism, and apriorism. The entry sorts empiricism into three chief forms: materialism, sensism, and positivism. Ancient atomists such as Democritus, Epicurus, and Lucretius reduced reality to atoms and motion, with knowledge made by images cast from objects into the soul. Modern materialists explain it by brain action instead, while sensists, from Empedocles and Protagoras onward, deny any real gap between sensations and ideas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-epicureanism:
Epicureanism has two distinct but kindred meanings, and this entry takes both in turn. In popular speech it means refined, calculating selfishness, chasing pleasures of sense, above all of the palate, in company rather than alone. An epicure is one extremely choice and delicate in his food. In its other sense it names a system of philosophy covering conduct, nature, and mind.

Epicurus, a Greek born at Samos in 341 before Christ, founded his school at Athens in 307 and died in 270. The Stoic school, its opposite, arose about the same time, probably in 310. Pleasure and Duty, the two watchwords, sprang up within a generation after Aristotle's death in 322. Epicurus laid down his principles dogmatically for pupils to learn by heart. That gave his school the unity of a sect or party rather than a debating society. Lucretius later sang the system in his poem On the Nature of Things.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-erastus-and-e:
Erastus and Erastianism takes up a name often used loosely for undue subservience of the Church to the State. That was not the principal question in Erastus's system, but a subsidiary deduction from it. The real name of Erastus was Thomas Lieber or Liebler. He was born at Baden in Switzerland, of humble parents, on 7 September 1524, and died on 31 December 1583.

He went to Basle in 1540, and two years later found a patron who helped him enter the university. His zeal for learning may be judged by this. Though disease took the use of his right arm, he learnt to write with his left hand, and took notes more fluently than others with no such impediment. Erastus caught the plague but did not suffer severely, and on recovery he left Basle for Bologna, where he studied philosophy and medicine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eunomianism:
Eunomianism was an extreme form of Arianism, the fourth-century teaching that denied the full divinity of Christ. It held sway among some Eastern churchmen from about 350 to 381. It took its name from Eunomius, disciple of Aetius, a former goldsmith, physician, and grammarian who argued from Aristotle's categories and the syllogism. Where orthodox Christians confessed the Son to be of the same substance as the Father, the Eunomians made unlike their watchword. They held the Son unlike the Father in substance and in all else.

The article follows the sect through favor at Antioch, condemnation by Semi-Arians at Ancyra and Sirmium, exile, and recall under Julian. It ends with final condemnation at the Council of Constantinople in 381, with Eunomius dying about 395. It also sets out his system: God, being simple and unbegotten, can be fully known, and since the Son is begotten, he must differ in substance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eutychianism:
Eutychianism is the name often given to Monophysitism, the teaching that Christ has one nature, not two, after the Incarnation. It prefers to use the words alike, since no party looked to Eutyches as founder, and Eutychian was a nickname for all who rejected the orthodox phrase two natures. The error grew as a reaction against Nestorianism, which seemed to split Christ into two persons.

Much of the article turns on words. It traces the peace of 434 between Cyril of Alexandria and John of Antioch. It also traces Cyril's phrase one nature incarnate of God the Word, and the double sense of the Greek word for nature. It follows the dispute through the Tome of Leo, the Council of Chalcedon, and the Fifth General Council. It shows how one formula, read in two ways, hardened into a lasting schism between churches that still confess it differently.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-exorcism:
Exorcism means two linked things. First, it is the act of driving out demons from persons, places, or things believed possessed or infested. Second, it is the means used for that end, above all solemn adjuration in the name of God. The word comes from exorkizo, used in the Septuagint for causing to swear and in Matthew for adjuring. Acts applies exorcist to strolling Jews who claimed power to cast out demons.

Among ethnic faiths, protective rites against spirits were everywhere. Egypt shows few strict exorcisms, though a god traveled from Thebes to free the Prince of Bekhten's daughter. Babylon tied exorcism to medicine, with formulas calling on heaven and earth to conjure demons away. The Old Testament shows no man expelling demons, though Tobias tells of an angel binding one. Later Jewish books give incantations, Solomon formulas, and the failed sons of Sceva.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fatalism:
Fatalism holds that every event, including each human action, is fixed by fate in advance. Ancient thinkers pictured fate as iron necessity, as divine decree, or as goddesses of destiny. Greek tragedy shows men borne along helplessly toward terrible ends. The Stoics taught an unbreakable chain of cause and effect with no room for chance.

Christianity reframed the problem as divine foreknowledge joined to human freedom. Moral responsibility requires that people can truly choose to keep or break the law. Islam stressed God's absolute decree, which some schools softened or denied. Buddhism, through past existences, leaves free will practically suppressed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-febronianism:
Febronianism was a politico-ecclesiastical system curbing papal power, set out in 1763. Johann Nikolaus von Hontheim wrote it as Justinus Febronius. He denied the Church's monarchical constitution and the pope's monarchical supremacy. His stated aim was reuniting Protestants by trimming Rome's sweeping claims.

Febronius gave the keys to the whole Church, with the pope first among prelates. The pope, he held, should keep only the essential rights of the first eight centuries. Councils, not the pope alone, would settle faith and discipline. His book fed Gallican and state-church movements across Catholic Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fetishism:
Fetishism means worship paid to material objects with supposed magic power. The word comes from Portuguese feitico, from the Latin factitius, made by art. Portuguese sailors found West Africans honouring small hand-made idols and amulets. De Brosses coined fetishism as a general term for early religion in 1760.

Comte made fetishism the lowest stage of man's religious development. Spencer and Tylor later placed it as a subdivision of animism instead. The fetish holds a spirit foreign to, yet embodied in, the object itself. Natives laughed at the idea of worshipping a mere stone for itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feudalism:
Feudalism was the land-based system of government of medieval Europe for seven centuries. The king let lands to men who paid their rent in governmental service. Service meant fighting, suit at the king's court, and local government work. Lords judged, taxed, and ruled the class next below them.

Its deep roots mixed Roman law, barbarian custom, and local usage. Diocletian's taxes drove free farmers under the protection of rich neighbours. The system faded as the cash-nexus replaced the land-nexus. Feudalism thus meant government by amateurs paid in land, not money.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fideism:
Fideism, from Latin fides, denies that unaided human reason can reach certitude. It makes faith, resting on authority, the supreme criterion of certitude. Moderate fideists still let reason show such belief reasonable after assent. Thinkers from Huet, Bonald, and Bautain to Lamennais held versions of this system.

Kant's split between pure reason and practical reason echoes this fideistic attitude. The Church repeatedly condemned fideistic theses from Nicholas d'Autrecourt in 1348 onward. Gregory XVI struck at Lamennais's ideas in 1832 and 1834. Trent and Vatican I affirmed reason's power to know God with certainty.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gallicanism:
Gallicanism names a set of French opinions that sought to restrain papal power in favor of bishops and kings. Its warmest friends never denied the pope's primacy nor claimed their views as articles of faith. They held only that their reading of Scripture and tradition fit the Church better, within the bounds of free theological opinion.

The system took official form in the Declaration of the French Clergy of 1682, in four articles. Popes hold power only over spiritual things, so kings cannot be deposed by church authority. The decrees of Constance stand firm. Papal power must follow the canons. And the laws and customs of the French kingdom and church keep their force, since the dignity of Rome itself demands that settled usages endure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gnosticism:
Gnosticism is the doctrine of salvation by knowledge, from gnosis, knowledge, and gnostikos, good at knowing. Where Judaism, Christianity, and almost all pagan systems hold that the soul reaches its end by obedience to the Supreme Power, Gnosticism places salvation merely in knowledge. That knowledge is quasi-intuitive, of the universe's mysteries and magic formulae. A Catholic Encyclopedia article gives the fuller historical definition of a collective name for many sects.

These greatly varying sects flourished from before the Christian Era to the fifth century. They borrowed the language and some tenets of the chief religions, especially Christianity. They held matter to be a deterioration of spirit and the universe a depravation of the Deity. The end of all being was overcoming matter's grossness and return to the Parent-Spirit, inaugurated by a God-sent Saviour. Their origins, debated, now seem to reach centuries before the Christian Era.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hedonism:
Hedonism holds that pleasure or happiness is the highest and final aim of conduct, so that actions are right insofar as they increase pleasure and wrong insofar as they increase pain. Its father was Aristippus of Cyrene, who counted mental pleasures, friendship, and moral contentment beside sensual delight, though his followers shrank the doctrine to self-indulgence.

Epicurus refined it toward social and intellectual pleasures with prudent self-restraint. English Utilitarians from Hobbes and Bentham to John Stuart Mill revived it as the greatest happiness of the greatest number. The entry's criticism calls the system false at root. Pleasure follows a good already sought, it is not the only motive, pleasures cannot be measured against one another, and egoistic hedonism turns benevolence into selfishness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hegelianism:
Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, born at Stuttgart in 1770, built a philosophy in which reality itself moves by triads: a concept passes into its opposite and returns richer than before. After Tübingen theology, tutoring, Jena, a Bamberg newspaper, a Nuremberg school. Heidelberg, he reached Berlin in 1818, publishing his Logic, Phenomenology of Spirit, and Encyclopedia.

Being, his Logic shows, slides into nothing and returns as becoming, the highest truth of a thing being its whole history, from tree to table to ashes. The same pattern runs through nature and mind. Logic studies the idea in itself, nature the idea out of itself, and mind the idea in and for itself, toward spirit, state, religion, and philosophy as its fullest forms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-herbart-and-h:
Johann Friedrich Herbart, born at Oldenburg in 1776, began logic at eleven, metaphysics at twelve, and studied philosophy under Fichte at Jena before elaborating his own system at twenty. After tutoring three sons of a nobleman and visiting Pestalozzi, he took his doctorate at Göttingen in 1802. In 1809 he succeeded to Kant's chair at Königsberg, founding a pedagogic seminary with a practice school where he taught daily for over twenty years.

In metaphysics Herbart defended realism against the idealism of his day. In psychology he replaced native faculties of soul with a simple soul bearing presentations whose interactions, he tried to quantify in numbers, indirectly stirring Fechner, Weber, and Wundt. His enduring interest was education: its end, set by ethics, is noble, moral character, formed through many-sided interest, apperception, and the five moral ideas of inner freedom, perfection, benevolence, right, and equity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hesychasm:
Hesychasm was a mystical system the monks of Mount Athos defended in the fourteenth century, and one of the strangest chapters in Byzantine church history. The word comes from the Greek for quiet. Hesychasts held that by strict asceticism, detachment from earthly cares, obedience to an approved master, and prayer in perfect repose of body and will, a monk could see a mystic light.

That light, they said, was nothing less than God's uncreated light, the same light seen at Christ's Transfiguration. It was not God's essence, which no one can see face to face in this life, but God's own eternal light. The entry explains the doctrine, then traces its stormy history, when an obscure speculation became a political party's watchword and tangled again with the old controversy against Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hinduism:
Hinduism, in its narrower sense, is the mass of religious beliefs and practices in India that grew out of ancient Brahminism. It now stands apart from orthodox, traditional Brahminism. In its broader sense it covers the religious, social, and intellectual life generally recognized in India as the legitimate outgrowth of ancient Brahmin institutions. Brahmin priests tolerate it as compatible with their traditions.

Far from one uniform system, Hinduism in the broad sense includes orthodox Brahminism plus many sectarian cults honouring Vishnu, Siva, and their associates. In those cults the great mass of people found religious satisfaction for centuries. What matters most is recognition of Brahmin supremacy and the sacredness of Brahmin customs. In the pantheistic all-god Brahma, the entry notes, every form of worship finds a place, from lofty monotheism to simple nature worship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-historical-cr:
Historical criticism is the art of telling the true from the false about facts of the past. It deals both with documents handed down to us and with the facts themselves. Its sources fall into three kinds: written documents, unwritten evidence, and tradition. Indirect research adds three more tools: negative argument, conjecture, and reasoning from first principles.

No study of sources avails much, the entry warns, without an ardent love of truth that guards against prejudice, religious, national, or domestic. The critic differs from an advocate: like an examining magistrate and an expert juryman at once, he must decide only on the fullest knowledge of details. Auxiliary sciences such as heraldry, numismatics, and linguistics each supply their own kinds of evidence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-humanism:
Humanism was the trend in thought, letters, and science in the fourteenth to sixteenth centuries that based every branch of learning on Greek and Roman books and culture. Believing only ancient training could form a perfect man, its friends named their cause against the scholastics and took humaniora, the humanities, as the learning of the ancients.

Though humanists saw the ages between antiquity and themselves as barbarous, their movement still linked to the past. Latin in church liturgy had prepared Europe for it, though medieval readers knew ancient books only through second-hand sources and feared their worldly view as a lure to sin. With a rising worldly turn, above all in wealthy, free Italian cities, those views changed. The entry traces humanism in Italy, Germany, and beyond, from Petrarch's circle to northern scholars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hylozoism:
Hylozoism, from Greek words for matter and life, is the doctrine that all matter possesses life. In its childish form it is simply the natural habit of reading our own life into other things, so children give life and soul to everything. Primitive races' personification of nature, also called animism, offers a poetical view of the world.

The first Greek philosophers, the Ionians, saw the universe as alive throughout and full of gods. With Anaxagoras, then Plato and Aristotle, matter and mind stood apart and their relations were mapped, and primitive hylozoism faded. With Strato of Lampsacus, Aristotle's second successor, a materialistic hylozoism returned: bodies alone are real, and life is a property of matter. Stoic doctrine likewise treated bodies alone as fully real.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hypnotism:
Hypnotism, from the Greek for sleep, means here the nervous sleep induced by artificial, external means, now studied methodically by scientists, physicians, and physiologists. It does not differ essentially from animal magnetism, which for a century won drawing-room success without forcing entry to scientific academies. Nor does it differ from Mesmerism or Braidism, explained in the article's history.

Hypnotism's causes remain debated, but one fact stands beyond question. A special sleep can be brought on by passes, by sharp or prolonged sensations, by sustained attention, or by an effort of will. Belief in a subtle, impalpable fluid, like mineral magnetism but peculiar to living beings, dates not from the eighteenth century but from high antiquity. Pliny, Galen, and Aretaeus all witness to that magnetic or vital fluid.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-iconoclasm:
Iconoclasm, or image-breaking, was the heresy that disturbed the Eastern Church in the eighth and ninth centuries. It brought the last of many breaks with Rome paving the way for Photius's schism. A smaller echo sounded in the West's Frankish kingdom. The Eastern story falls into two separate persecutions of Catholics.

At the end of each persecution stands an image-venerating empress, Irene and then Theodora. The movement's origins have been much debated. Some trace it to Muslim influence, since Muslims abhor any picture or statue of the human form, and the caliph at Damascus applauded the iconoclast emperors. Yet the entry doubts the chief cause lay in the example of a bitter enemy, and traces the emperors' own zeal against pictures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-idealism:
Idealism turns on the Greek idea, meaning image, figure, or form, which can mean likeness or copy as well as type, model, or pattern. That latter sense lives in ideal and the ideal. The ideal copies no perceptible object; it is a type, and an artist idealizes a subject by showing it fairer, nobler, and more perfect than reality.

Idealism in life marks those who take truth, right, goodness, and beauty as standards and guiding forces, a sense shaped by Plato, who made idea a technical term. For Plato the visible world merely copies a supersensible, intelligible, ideal world, and things are impressions stamped on reality by a higher, spiritual nature. Platonism is idealism's oldest form, and the entry follows its later shapes through modern philosophy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-individualism:
No neat definition will hold this term, the entry warns at the outset, since it is not simply the opposite of socialism. A dictionary sense that limits it to a theory of government favoring non-interference by the state covers only its political or civic form. The entry offers a broader sketch instead: a pull toward personal liberty against outside authority, and toward solo action against joint action.

Outside authority here means more than governments, political or religious. It takes in voluntary groups and the shared standards of conduct and belief that press on a person. A worker who refuses a union on principle, a reformer who trusts single actors over social methods, and a writer who drops accepted rules all illustrate the pull. The entry sorts those cases without forcing them into one creed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jainism:
Jainism is a religion standing between Brahminism and Buddhism in form. It arose in India before Christian times. It has kept a heretical stance toward Brahminism down to the present day. Its name comes from jina, or conqueror, an epithet for its reputed founder. Jainism closely resembles Buddhism in monastic system, ethical teaching, sacred texts, and founder's story.

That closeness led scholars such as Lassen, Weber, Wilson, Tiele, and Barth to view Jainism as Buddhism's offshoot. They placed its origin some centuries after Buddha. The prevailing view today, held by Bühler, Jacobi, Hopkins, and others, treats Jainism as independent of Buddhism in origin. It may even be the older of the two. Shared points, on that view, come from both sects' debts to a common Indian heritage. The entry weighs a classic question of religious origins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jansenius-and:
Cornelius Jansen, bishop of Ypres, gives Jansenism its origin and name. He must not be confused with another writer and bishop of the same name, Cornelius Jansenius Gandavensis, who lived from 1510 to 1576. That elder Jansen wrote several books on Scripture and a valuable Concordia Evangelica. The subject of this article lived three-quarters of a century later. He was born on 28 October 1585, of a Catholic family, in Accoi village near Leerdam, Holland. He died at Ypres on 6 May 1638.

His parents, though in moderate circumstances, secured him an excellent education. They sent him first to Utrecht. In 1602 he entered Louvain university's Falcon College to study philosophy. There he spent two years. At the solemn promotion of 1604 he was proclaimed first among 118 competitors. To begin theology he entered Louvain's theological faculty. The entry opens the life of a scholar whose posthumous Augustinus sparked a century of French church conflict.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-judaism:
Judaism is the religious communion that outlived Assyria's and Babylon's destruction of the Jewish nation. This long entry surveys it under four heads: Judaism before the Christian era, Judaism and early Christianity, Judaism since AD 70, and Judaism and Church legislation.

After the return from Babylon in 538 BC, the exiles resolved to keep the Law in purity, having learned from captivity that God punished idolatry and rewarded faithfulness. Ezra's public reading of the Law set their calling as a priestly kingdom and holy nation before them. The entry follows that resolve through later ages to modern Church law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-knownothingis:
Knownothingism was the name of an American political movement loud from 1851 to 1858. It revived the older Native American movement, whose aims were to bar Roman Catholics from public office and shut foreign-born citizens out of posts of trust and profit.

Irish Catholics, native or immigrant, drew the sharpest hostility, and most targeted foreigners were Irish Catholic immigrants. The article traces the spirit back to colonial penal laws against Catholic worship, then to the Constitution's ban on religious tests and the 1791 amendment guarding free exercise. States, however, kept control of religion at home, and their Catholic disqualifications faded only slowly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liberalism:
Liberalism means a free way of thinking and acting. The word liberal comes from Latin liber, free, and until the end of the eighteenth century meant only worthy of a free man, as in liberal arts and liberal occupations.

The word has covered such tendencies since the late eighteenth century, however, in intellectual, religious, political, and economic life. These imply man's freedom from the supernatural, moral, and divine order. Its most basic principle asserts absolute freedom of conscience, creed, speech, press, politics, religion, and thought. From this follow the abolition of Divine right and of every authority derived from God. Religion is pushed out of public life into private conscience, and Christianity and the Church are ignored as public institutions. It also follows that every man gains absolute autonomy, and all public authority gathers into one sovereignty of the people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lutherans-and:
Lutherans and Lutheranism are the faith of the oldest and, in Europe, largest Protestant body, founded by Martin Luther of Wittenberg. Foes coined Lutheran at the Leipzig Disputation in 1519, though Luther preferred Evangelical, and the church today calls itself Evangelical Lutheran.

Official doctrine keeps Scripture and the three ancient creeds: Apostles', Nicene, and Athanasian. Six Lutheran confessions join them: Augsburg of 1530, its Apology, Luther's two catechisms, the Smalkald Articles, and the Form of Concord. Together they form the Book of Concord of 1580. Justification, how a sinner stands right with God, stands as the article on which the church stands or falls, and the survey follows its spread, rites, and divisions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-manichaeism:
Manichaeism was a religion founded by the Persian Mani in the later third century. It claimed to blend all known faiths into one true synthesis. In fact it mixed Zoroastrian dualism, Babylonian lore, Buddhist ethics, and a thin Christian veneer. 

Mani first preached his gospel on 20 March 242, after steeping himself in Babylon's pagan priestly lore. His cosmogony tells of light invaded by darkness, a First Man sent to fight, and light substance trapped in matter that must be freed. The Perfect few kept strict discipline, with prayer four times daily, while hearers lived more loosely. Mani called himself the Paraclete and rejected the Old Testament, keeping only parts of the New. Despite fierce persecution by Sassanids and Roman emperors, the faith raced east and west, lingering in the West for a thousand years and flourishing in Mesopotamia, Turkestan, India, China, and Tibet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-materialism:
Materialism holds that matter alone is real, that all events come from matter at work, and thus denies God and the soul. It stands against views that call all things spirit and matter mere thought. Materialism is older than Spiritualism if philosophy begins in Greece, though ancient Indian thought was idealistic, with Brahma alone real.

In Greece the first thinkers leaned this way, and Socrates's school pushed back. Lucretius gave Epicurus's version poetic voice. Christianity dammed materialism mightily, until Renaissance humanists revived antiquity. In Germany Leibniz assailed it vigorously, while Fichte, Hegel, and Schelling called matter a mind's projection. Natural science's triumphs then bolstered materialism, and Darwinism seemed to settle design questions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mechanism:
Mechanism, a term with no fixed sense in the history of philosophy, first named the view that the world's motion and change come from some outside force. In that view, material things are purely passive. The rival view, Dynamism, grants things inner sources of energy that drive their acts and their effects on events. Soon the debate shifted, and many thinkers set aside whether motion is built into bodies or handed to them.

For a large school, Mechanism reduces all qualities and acts of bodies to mass and motion. A further shift carried the theory into life itself: it seeks to explain all vital events as physical and chemical facts, with reduction to mass and motion as a secondary hope. Against this biological Mechanism stands Vitalism, or Neo-vitalism, which holds that living acts can never be explained in lifeless terms. The entry sets out arguments, criticism, and conclusion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mendel-mendel:
Gregor Johann Mendel, born at Heinzendorf near Odrau in Austrian Silesia in 1822, died at the Augustinian Abbey of St. Thomas, Brunn, in 1884. His father was a small peasant farmer of scant means. A younger sister gave up much of her dowry so the family could school him, a debt he later repaid and more. After Leipnik school he shone so brightly that his parents sent him to Troppau gymnasium and then to Olmutz.

At Troppau one teacher was an Augustinian, and in 1843 Mendel sought the novitiate at Brunn's Abbey of St. Thomas. Ordained in 1847, he taught until 1851, when he went to Vienna for two years of maths, physics, and natural science. Returning in 1853, he taught physics at the Realschule for fifteen years. The entry follows his life and the laws of heredity his garden work revealed, the Mendelism that later reshaped biology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-methodism:
Methodism is a religious movement begun in 1739 by John Wesley inside the Anglican Church, which later bore many separate denominations. Wesley and Methodism treated religion as practical first, not dogmatic, which likely explains the lack of any formal Methodist creed. The General Rules, issued by John and Charles Wesley on 1 May 1743, set the terms for joining their United Societies, almost wholly practical, demanding no doctrinal test.

Yet Methodism built its own theology on two chief standards. The first is the Twenty-five Articles of religion, an abridgment of the Church of England's Thirty-nine Articles, and the only doctrinal standard strictly binding American Methodists. Wesley prepared twenty-four for the American Church, adopted at Baltimore in 1784, and Article XXIII, recognizing American political independence, was added in 1804. The second standard is the first fifty-three of Wesley's published sermons with his Notes on the New Testament.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-millennium-an:
Millenarianism, as Christian writers understand it, holds that at the end of time Christ will return in splendour, gather the just, destroy hostile powers, and found a glorious kingdom on earth. He himself will reign as king, and all the just, including saints recalled to life, will share its highest spiritual and material blessings. At the kingdom's close the saints will enter heaven with Christ.

The wicked, also raised, will face eternal damnation. This reign is commonly given as one thousand years, hence millennium, though a thousand years is not essential to the idea. The article traces the belief from the Gnostic Cerinthus, who pictured the thousand years in gross sensual colours, through Papias of Hierapolis, to later Catholic and sectarian forms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mithraism:
Mithraism was a pagan religion centred on the cult of Mithra, the ancient Indo-Iranian sun god. It entered Europe from Asia Minor after Alexander's conquest. It spread rapidly over the whole Roman Empire at the beginning of our era and reached its zenith in the third century. It vanished under the repressive laws of Theodosius at the end of the fourth century. Of late Cumont's researches have brought it into prominence.

Its origin dates from when Hindus and Persians still formed one people, for Mithra appears in both religions. The Roman cult, practised chiefly by soldiers, centred on Mithra's slaying of the bull in underground temples called mithraea. Its supposed likeness to Christianity, in meals, baptism, and a saviour god, has been much debated, though the parallels are often overstated.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-modernism:
Modernism, by its roots, means too much love of what is new. As a church term it denotes a system condemned by Pius X in the early twentieth century. Its core fault, as the article presents it, lies in making church teaching the fruit of man's inward felt life, not of God's word from above.

It treats doctrines as changing with the times, rather than as fixed truth. The movement drew on Kant's thought and the new Bible study, and its chief figures included Loisy in France and Tyrrell in England. After debate even among good Catholics, the decree Lamentabili in 1907 condemned sixty-five Modernist propositions. The encyclical Pascendi of 8 September 1907, De Modernistarum doctrinis, set out and condemned the system as a whole.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-molinism:
Molinism is a school of Catholic theology that tries to hold two claims together. God's grace works unfailingly, yet the human will stays genuinely free. The Spanish Jesuit Luis de Molina first worked it out, and the Society of Jesus took it up. It answers the rival Thomist school, which starts instead from the power of efficacious grace.

At its heart lies middle knowledge. That is the idea that God knows what any free person would do under conditions that never occur. The people of Tyre and Sidon, for instance, would have repented at miracles they never saw. The entry traces the long dispute with the Thomists and the arguments over grace and consent defined at Trent. The two schools tunnelled from opposite sides, yet never quite met.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monasticism:
Monasticism, from Greek words for dwelling alone, means a life of seclusion from the world. It is lived under religious vows and a fixed rule by monks, friars and nuns. Its core idea is withdrawal, pursued through self-denial and ordered asceticism. It aims at a life sharply different from the one most people lead.

The entry argues that this pattern appears in every highly developed faith. Brahmin, Buddhist, Jewish, Christian and Muslim traditions all show it, and even modern communal societies do. That suggests it answers something deep in human nature alongside domestic life. Companion articles trace the Eastern and Western forms in detail, from desert hermits and the rules of Basil and Benedict to the mendicant orders and later congregations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monism:
Monism, from the Greek word for one, is the philosophical claim that reality at bottom is a single thing. It stands against dualism, which splits body from soul or matter from spirit. It also stands against pluralism, which holds many things real. Where others see a genuine many, the monist sees phases or appearances of one underlying unity.

The entry traces the idea from Hindu teachers, who called the world of sense illusion and held God alone real. It moves to the Eleatics of early Greece, who argued that Being is one, changeless and eternal. It follows monism through medieval and modern thought. It weighs materialist, idealist and pantheist versions. It tests each against the Catholic view that God, soul and matter remain distinct even while God sustains them all.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monophysites-:
Monophysites held that Christ has a single nature after the Incarnation. This long entry takes up two questions left aside in the companion article on Eutychianism. The first is their literary output in Greek and Syriac. The second is whether their Christology can be excused from real heresy. No early heresy before the sixteenth century produced so vast a literature. Much of it is lost or survives only in manuscript.

Greek works largely perished in their original form but live on in early Syriac translations. Syriac writing survives in greater bulk. It covers church history, biography, dogma and polemic across the fifth and sixth centuries and beyond. The entry surveys leading authors from Dioscurus onward. It weighs their arguments about Christ's nature and will. It judges how far language, rather than doctrine, divided them from the councils.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monotheism:
Monotheism, a modern coinage from Greek words for only and god, means belief in one supreme God. That God is Creator and Lord of the world, eternal, all-powerful, all-wise and all-good. He rewards good and punishes evil. The belief stands against polytheism, belief in many gods, and atheism, belief in none. It differs from deism and pantheism by holding God both distinct from the world and active within it.

The entry sets out reason's grounds for one God. It then asks whether monotheism was humanity's first religion. It weighs evolutionist claims of a slow climb from lower beliefs against evidence for an early knowledge of one God. It surveys monotheism among the Hebrews, in ancient philosophy and in Islam. It argues that Christian revelation gives the doctrine its fullest force and clarity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mormonism:
Mormonism, also called the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, began in the early nineteenth century under Joseph Smith. Smith, son of a Vermont farmer, was born at Sharon on 23 December 1805. Troubled over his salvation during a revival that drew kin toward Presbyterianism, he prayed for guidance. He claimed a visitation from two glorious beings who told him to join none of the existing churches.

On the night of 21 September 1823, he said, the messenger Moroni revealed an ancient record. It held Christ's teaching to the Nephites, a branch of Israel that had lived in America long before Columbus. From the plates Smith dictated the Book of Mormon and organised the church in 1830. He led his followers through Ohio, Missouri and Illinois to Utah. The entry weighs the movement's doctrines, polygamy and history from a Catholic standpoint.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mysticism:
Mysticism, from a Greek verb meaning to initiate, implies a relation to mystery. In philosophy it is either a religious tendency of the soul toward intimate union with the Divinity, or a system growing from that desire. As a system it makes the soul's direct union with God through contemplation and love the end of philosophy. It seeks the processes and means of reaching that end.

That contemplation, in its account, is not merely analogical knowledge of the Infinite but a direct and immediate intuition of it. Mysticism may be speculative or practical, contemplative or affective, orthodox or heterodox, by its emphasis and its agreement with Catholic teaching. Cousin counted it among four systems between which thought has wavered, with Sensism, Idealism and Scepticism. The entry sketches its history and influence, then criticises it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-naturalism:
Naturalism is less a special system than a point of view or tendency shared by many philosophical and religious systems. It is less a fixed set of doctrines than an attitude pervading many doctrines. As the name implies, it treats nature as the one original source of all that exists, and tries to explain everything in terms of nature.

Either nature's limits are reality's limits, or a first cause, if needed, has nothing to do with natural agencies. All events thus find adequate explanation within nature. Since nature bears more than one sense, naturalism lacks one fixed meaning. In its physical sense it makes the material universe the only reality, reducing laws to mechanical uniformities and denying spirit-matter dualism. In other senses it admits mind and matter as modes of one substance. The entry sorts the varieties and criticises them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-naturism:
Naturism is the term Reville proposed for the worship of nature. It differs from naturalism, an atheistic philosophy rather than a religion. It also differs from natural religion, the truths about God and man reachable by reason alone, such as God's existence, the soul's immortality, and the moral order. As a theory of religion, naturism shows three phases: ethnographic, philosophic, and science-naturism.

Ethnographic naturism, in Reville's account, is religion's primitive form, the basis of all existing forms, as the study of myths supposedly shows. It rests on two ideas. The philosophic idea of evolution makes early man a creature of emotion rather than intelligence. The ethnographic idea holds that early man lived as today's non-civilised races do. The entry tests those assumptions, surveys nature worship, and judges naturism's claims.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-neo-platonism:
Neo-Platonism is a system of idealistic, spiritualistic philosophy tending toward mysticism, which flourished in the pagan Greek and Roman world during the first Christian centuries. It matters not only as Greek thought's last attempt to restore its exhausted vitality through Oriental religious ideas, but because it entered pagan polytheism's service as a weapon against Christianity. Its first representatives drew inspiration from Plato, though many treatises they trusted are not genuine Plato.

It arose in Egypt, a sign that, while a product of the Hellenistic spirit, it drew heavily on Oriental religious ideals and mystic tendencies. Its founders pursued a twofold purpose, since Stoicism, Epicureanism, Eclecticism and even Scepticism had failed at moral and religious regeneration. The entry traces the system from Plotinus through Porphyry, Iamblichus and Proclus, its doctrines of the One, Intellect and Soul, and Christianity's response.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-neo-scholasti:
Neo-Scholasticism is the development of medieval Scholasticism during the later nineteenth century. It is not merely the revival of a long-defunct philosophy, but a restatement today of the perennial philosophy. That philosophy was elaborated by the Greeks and perfected by the great medieval teachers, never wholly extinct even in modern times. It is sometimes called neo-Thomism, since Saint Thomas Aquinas gave Latin Scholasticism its final form in the thirteenth century.

Thomism alone is too narrow a name, since the system is too large for any single exponent. The entry covers the elements neo-Scholasticism takes from the past, the modifications adapting it to the present, its welcome among contemporary thinkers, and its outlook. It names its leading representatives and centres, and argues that truth from seven hundred years ago remains true today, and philosophy does not shift with each passing phase of history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nestorius-and:
Nestorius, who gave his name to the Nestorian heresy, was born at Germanicia in Syria and died in the Egyptian Thebaid about 451. A priest and monk at Euprepius near the walls, he was chosen by Theodosius II as Patriarch of Constantinople after Sisinnius, famed for eloquence. He was consecrated in April 428 and at once showed zeal against heretics, destroying an Arian chapel and pressing severe edicts.

He seized Macedonian churches, moved against Quartodecimans and Novatians, yet spared Pelagian refugees, whose condemnation he barely knew. His teaching divided Christ into two persons, denying Mary the title Mother of God, and Cyril of Alexandria opposed him. The Council of Ephesus in 431 condemned and deposed him. The entry follows his exile, his writings, and the Nestorian church's spread through Persia, India and China.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nihilism:
Nihilism, the Russian movement that bowed to no authority and no doctrine without proof, grew from revolt against tsarist absolutism. Turgenev coined the name in Fathers and Sons in 1862. Chernyshevsky sketched a new order on the ruins of the old, and the Decembrist rising of 1825 gave the cause its first martyrs.

Herzen and Bakunin carried the theory abroad through journals like Kolokol, students spread it in universities, and later nihilists turned from argument to bombs and assassinations. The entry traces that slide from philosophy to terror under Alexander II and Alexander III.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nominalism-re:
Nominalism, realism, and conceptualism name rival answers to philosophy's problem of universals: how general ideas in the mind match real things outside it. Objects are single and definite, the entry notes, while our concepts are abstract and shared, so thinkers must explain what, if anything, a universal term truly stands for.

Exaggerated realism gives universals a reality of their own, nominalism leaves them as mere names, conceptualism places them in the mind, and moderate realism threads between. The entry surveys ancient and medieval forms of each view and defends the moderate path.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-novatian-and-:
Novatian, a third-century Roman priest who made himself antipope, founded a rigorist sect that refused pardon to Christians who lapsed in persecution. Baptized by affusion on a sickbed as a catechumen and never confirmed, he still rose to the priesthood despite protests that his ordination broke canon law.

When Cornelius became pope in 251, Novatian's backers consecrated him rival bishop, and his followers, called Novatians or Cathari, kept separate churches for centuries. The entry weighs his learning and eloquence against Cornelius's charge that ambition, not doctrine, drove the schism. Cornelius sarcastically called him a maker of dogmas and champion of ecclesiastical learning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-occasionalism:
Occasionalism holds that finite things cause nothing by themselves, and that God alone acts, with creatures serving as mere occasions for divine action. An occasion lures or prompts the true cause, as a final cause drawing action or a lesser cause nudging a greater one to act.

Foreshadowed by Stoics who saw God pervading nature, the theory surfaced in medieval Arab thought and matured among Cartesians puzzled by mind-body union. Since thought and extension share nothing, Malebranche and others made God the link, producing every sensation and motion on the occasion of bodily states.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-occult-art-oc:
Occult art, or occultism, covers practices that seek hidden power over nature by means inadequate on their face. The entry treats magic proper, setting aside animism, astrology, divination, and fetishism to their own articles, and traces the word from Sumerian imga through Persian magi to Greek magos.

Magic tries to bend nature by formulas, gestures, and strange mixtures learned through secret traffic with forces behind the universe, rather than by God's free gift in miracle. Despairing of moving God by prayer, its adepts chase results through hidden powers, and the entry judges the art by theology and history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ontologism:
Ontologism claims that God and divine ideas form the first object of the mind, and that intuition of God opens all intellectual knowledge. Malebranche built the theory in his Search after Truth under Platonic and Cartesian sway, misunderstanding Augustine and Aquinas on the origin of ideas.

Ideas, on this view, are not elaborations of sense but archetypes in God, the infinite model that temporal things realize. We see all things in him as bodies lie in space. The entry traces the system's growth, its link to occasional causes, and the church's cautions against it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-optimism:
Optimism, from the Latin for best, names both a metaphysical theory and a temper of mind. The term spread in the early eighteenth century for Leibniz's view of this world as the best of all possible ones, against pessimism's claim that the world is on the whole bad.

Between those poles lie shades, including meliorism, Sully's word for the view that things are bad but can improve through human effort. As a temper, optimism looks on the bright side through inner constitution more than fortune, and the entry weighs how temper has swayed philosophers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-origen-and-or:
Origen, the Alexandrian scholar born in 185, shaped Christian thought more than any writer of his age, and Origenism names the controversies his ideas later stirred. Barely seventeen when persecution killed his father Leonides, Origen wrote from hiding urging his father to persevere, then taught grammar and Scripture in Alexandria.

Eusebius, who kept Origen's library at Caesarea and his letters, tells his life in full, with Gregory Thaumaturgus's farewell address beside it. The entry follows Origen to Caesarea, his Hexapla, his allegorical reading, and the later condemnations that shadowed his fame.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paganism:
Paganism, in the widest sense, covers every religion besides the one revealed by God, and in a narrower sense every faith besides Christianity, Judaism, and Mohammedanism. The word also serves as a synonym for polytheism, belief in many gods. It comes from the Latin pagus, a country district, since country folk, the pagani, stayed heathen after cities turned Christian.

Special articles treat faiths like Brahminism, Buddhism, and Mithraism. This entry handles paganism in general: its claims to count as religion, its grip on public and private life, its schools and morals, and its links with education and the state. It argues that historians posit a common germ, totemism or nature worship, yet history shows each faith already formed and complex. It closes by marking the gulf between pagan mysteries and Christian dogma and rite.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-palm-in-chris:
The palm stood in pre-Christian days as a sign of victory, and early Christians took it up as a sign of the faithful beating the soul's foes. Origen calls it the mark of victory in the spirit's war against the flesh. It fitted martyrs best, the chief victors over mankind's spiritual enemies, hence the phrase palm of martyrdom in martyr acts.

On 10 April 1688 the Congregation of Rites ruled that a palm on a catacomb tomb proved a martyr lay there. Mabillon, Muratori, Benedict XIV, and others later judged that view unsound, since palms appear on post-persecution and even pagan tombs. The palm's sense shifts with its neighbours, beside the monogram of Christ, the Fish, or the Good Shepherd, and on later stones it serves merely as ornament between scenes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-panpsychism:
Panpsychism is the philosophical theory that everything in the universe, inorganic as well as organic, holds some degree of consciousness. It stands close to hylozoism, the teaching that all matter is alive, and Paul Carus coined panbiotism to mark his own view off from Haeckel's panpsychism. Ancient hylozoists already treated the spirits of matter and plants as alive and more or less conscious.

Renaissance nature philosophers and alchemists revived the old view, musing on spirits, feelings, and strivings in all things. Leibniz's monads are plainly panpsychist: every monad is conscious and mirrors the whole universe, differing only in clarity. The modern school began with Fechner, from 1801 to 1887, and gained fresh push from Darwinian thought in England and metaphysical speculation in America. Later pages weigh its proofs and faults.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pantheism:
Pantheism is the view that God and the world are one. John Toland coined the name pantheist in his Socinianism Truly Stated of 1705, his opponent Fay first used pantheism in 1709, and Toland printed his Pantheisticon in 1732. The doctrine itself reaches back to early Indian thought and recurs in many shapes through history, so that, as Flint notes, no pure pantheism likely exists.

In its strictest sense, naming God and the world as one, pantheism is simply atheism. Every form holds monism, one sole being, necessary, eternal, and infinite, beneath the world's apparent many. Two questions then arise: what is this being, and how do manifold appearances arise? Answers run through Brahminism, Stoicism, Neo-Platonism, Gnosticism, Eriugena, Bruno, and Spinoza, whose system the entry treats at length.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-parallelism:
Parallelism is the balancing of verse with verse, a core mark of Hebrew poetry. By repetition, antithesis, or other devices, thought is set against thought and form against form, driving meaning home with force and grace. Assyrian and Babylonian hymns show the same ground pattern, and Schrader assumed Hebrew poets borrowed it from them.

A shared Semitic source from before Abraham's migration seems likelier. Syriac, Vulgate, and other old versions kept the balance in part, but only in the sixteenth century did Hebrew scholars name it a poetic principle. Rabbi Azaria de Rossi first split poetic passages into verses showing the balance, and Schoettgen first framed its canons as exergasia, the working up of a theme. Later pages sort its kinds and laws.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pelagius-and-:
Pelagianism was a fifth-century teaching that denied original sin and the need for divine grace. It took its name from the British monk Pelagius. This long Catholic Encyclopedia entry opens with what little is known of his life. He was a tall, learned lay monk who lived in Rome for years, wrote fluently in Latin and Greek, and held a reputation for strict self-discipline before leaving the city in 411.

Most of the article follows the storm that followed. Augustine of Hippo answered Pelagius and his ally Caelestius, and synods at Jerusalem, Carthage, and Rome weighed the charges. Popes Innocent I and Zosimus shifted position before the teaching was condemned in 418. Later chapters trace its afterlife through Julian of Eclanum, its lingering hold in Britain, Ireland, and Italy, and its final defeat at the Second Synod of Orange in 529.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pessimism:
Pessimism means two linked things: a gloomy temper, and a philosophy that judges existence itself as evil. In common speech the pessimist dwells on pain and lightly values pleasure, a cast of mind the entry traces to natural disposition, hard circumstance, and ages of transition when old certainties loosen. Poets from Lucretius to Aeschylus gave the mood its classic voice, with life itself counted a failure.

As a system, pessimism begins with Schopenhauer, for whom evil is not an accident of nature but its very ground. Hartmann reworked him, grounding reality in the unconscious, where will and idea work as twin functions. The entry tests both thinkers against Christian teaching. Duty, it argues, gives even painful action a worth beyond pleasure. For all their gloom, the systems sharpen the question of life's value.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pestalozzi-an:
Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi was a Swiss pioneer of modern education, born at Zurich in 1746. Raised for the pulpit in a Calvinist family, he turned instead to law, fell under Rousseau's spell, and tried farming at Neuhof. Farming failed, but in 1774 he gathered poor children there to work his spinning mill and gain industrial and moral training. That venture closed in 1780, leaving him and his wife at times without bread or fuel.

Fame came with his 1781 village tale Lienhard und Gertrud, showing a community remade by pastor, magistrate, teacher, and a good mother. In 1798 he took charge of orphans at Stanz after French troops burned the village. His methods spread through Prussia, England, and America, where Joseph Neef opened a Philadelphia school in 1808 and Horace Mann carried the principles onward. He died at Brugg in 1827.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-phenomenalism:
Phenomenalism is the view that knowledge reaches only appearances, never the thing itself. This Catholic Encyclopedia study gives the term two shapes: denial that substance can be known in the metaphysical sense, and denial that any reality stands apart from consciousness at all. The first shape reaches full statement in Hume, though its roots run through Berkeley and Locke to Descartes.

For Hume, substance is only a relation among ideas, a fictitious permanent ground the imagination invents to tie fleeting impressions together. Association of ideas explains consciousness without it, and metaphysics gives way to epistemology. Later sections follow the doctrine through Kant and his successors, weighing what phenomenalism gains in rigour against what it surrenders: a world beyond the mind.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philanthropin:
Philanthropinism was an education system drawn from Rousseau and the German Enlightenment and founded by Johann Bernhard Basedow on philanthropy. A Hamburg schoolboy under the freethinker Reimarus, Basedow studied theology at Leipzig, tutored in Holstein, and taught at Soroe in Denmark until rationalist opinions cost him his post in 1761. At Altona he wrote his Methodenbuch of 1770 for improving schools.

Prince Leopold of Anhalt-Dessau called him to Dessau, where his Elementarwerk of 1774 paired pictures with ideas after Comenius's Orbis pictus. In 1774 he opened the Philanthropinum, a model school of kindness: gentle discipline, attractive lessons, and easy study replaced the old severity. Basedow's pupils and imitators carried the system across Germany, though his own restless temper soon left the school to others.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pietism:
Pietism was a Protestant movement that sought to revive heartfelt devotion and practical Christian living. It arose against dry seventeenth-century orthodoxy and took shape in the German Lutheran church around 1670. It is linked above all to Philipp Jakob Spener, though kindred stirrings had already appeared among Dutch Reformed believers and on the Lower Rhine.

At Frankfurt, where Spener became pastor in 1666, he preached a living faith and holiness in daily life. In 1670 he opened private gatherings in his house for prayerful reading and mutual encouragement, called colleges of piety. His Pia desideria of 1675 set out the programme, and the entry traces its forerunners, its spread, and its later course.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-plato-and-pla:
Plato and Platonism covers the life, writings, and philosophy of Plato, the Athenian thinker born in 428 or 427 B.C. Of aristocratic family, he met Socrates about the age of twenty, and their eight or ten years together fixed the course of his thought. That friendship absorbed his early poetry and political hopes into the pursuit of wisdom.

After Socrates' death he travelled in Egypt, Italy, and Sicily and studied the Pythagoreans. He tried in vain to steer the rulers of Syracuse toward his ideal state, suffering prison and sale into slavery before friends ransomed him. Back at Athens he taught in the groves of Academus until his death near eighty, leaving dialogues such as the Republic, Phaedo, and Banquet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-polytheism: Polytheism is the belief in, and consequent worship of, many gods. This entry is a cross-reference stub. It does not develop a doctrine of its own. It points readers to articles on national religions: Assyrian, Babylonian, Hindu, and the ancient faiths of Egypt, Greece, and Rome. It also points to animism, fetishism, totemism, God, monotheism, and pantheism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-positivism:
Positivism is the set of philosophic and religious doctrines worked out by Auguste Comte. As a philosophy, it denies metaphysical speculation and holds sense experience the sole object and test of knowledge. As a religion, it denies a personal God and worships humanity, the great being. Comte was born at Montpellier on 19 January 1798 and died at Paris on 5 September 1857. He entered the Ecole Polytechnique in 1814 and began to print his course of philosophy in 1826.

An unhappy marriage and his love for Mme Clotilde de Vaux in 1845 and 1846 shaped his bent. He came to see that mere growth of mind falls short for life, and, having set Positivism out as a science, he aimed to make it a religion of humanity. The entry then weighs his claims: sense alone cannot bar causes and laws past single facts, nor shut out beings reason can infer as causes of what is.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-poverty-and-p:
In law, pauperism means the state of folk kept at public cost, in or out of almshouses. In common use it covers all whose life rests for a good while on charity, public or private. Poverty is vaguer and more relative. In Catholic teaching and ascetic use, it means giving up the right to own things, as in the vow of poverty and the poor in spirit of the Sermon on the Mount. Like pauperism, it spells a lasting state, and need not imply charity received.

Known causes run: drink, loose living, crime, thriftlessness, want of skill, heredity and company, low wages and want of work, inborn defects, harmful trades, sickness, mishap, and old age. Each can breed want alone, and each can breed or feed another. Its fruits are bodily pain, moral decay, dull minds, weak work, harm to society, and at last more want.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pragmatism:
Pragmatism, as a bent in philosophy, tests truth by use and by practical fruits. On its negative side it wars on the formalism of Intellectualist thought. Notions, judgments, and trains of reason, it says, do not mirror reality and its workings. On its positive side it sets up a test that is not of reason. Action, the meeting of needs, carrying out in conduct, or the chance to live a thought may serve, and reality is judged by that norm alone.

Kant's sway is plain: Descartes, with I think, therefore I exist, fathered Intellectualism. Kant swapped ought for think, moral mind for theoretic mind, and from that swap sprang a brood of will based, non rational schools. Bergson presses the same point on science: reality is a stream, a living flow. To use notions as meant, we must keep them in the stream, that is, live them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-predestinaria:
Predestinarianism is a heresy met oft. It traces the elect's eternal bliss and the reprobate's eternal doom to one cause alone: the sovereign will of God. It thus shuts out man's free working with grace as a second cause of his happy or unhappy lot to come. Its root claims are two. God's absolute will alone causes bliss or doom, with no heed to man's merits or faults. For the elect it denies free will under efficacious grace, while it lays on the reprobate a need to sin, since grace is withheld.

The system runs thus: why some are saved and others damned can only be met by an eternal, absolute, changeless decree of God. Bliss and doom are simply the fruit of an unconditional decree. History offers the pseudo Augustine text that gave Pelagians an opening to assail one sided views and true Augustinian teaching on grace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-presbyteriani:
Presbyterianism, broadly, is church rule by representative assemblies called presbyteries. It stands against rule by bishops, the episcopal system, and against rule by congregations, the congregational way. Churches shaped by the Swiss Reformation carry the Reformed name when Swiss, Dutch, or partly German. The French are Huguenots, the Bohemian and Hungarian bodies go by national names, and the Scotch, English, and derived churches are Presbyterian. Many joined the 1876 Alliance of Reformed Churches holding the Presbyterian System.

Orthodox Presbyterian standards are chiefly the Westminster Confession of Faith and Catechisms of 1647, though churches have altered their contents, and subscription rules oft ask but a qualified assent. In Ireland, Presbyterianism began with the Presbytery of Ulster in 1642, but Stuart restoration in 1660 checked its growth. In the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, drift from old standards and Unitarian leanings split the Ulster Presbyterians, and two Irish Presbyterian bodies remain Unitarian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-priscillianis:
Priscillianism arose in fourth-century Spain from Gnostic-Manichaean doctrines taught by Memphis's Egyptian Marcus. His first followers were Agape and the rhetorician Helpidius. Through them Priscillian, a man of noble birth and great riches, joined the party. His rank and gifts made him the party's leader. His gifts of speech and his name for harsh asceticism drew a large following, among them the bishops Instantius and Salvianus.

The sect bound itself by oath, and its swift spread caught the eye of Hyginus, Bishop of Cordova, who warned Idacius of Emerita. At Idacius's and Ithacius of Ossanova's instance, a synod met at Saragossa in 380, with bishops from Spain and Aquitaine. The Priscillianists stayed away, and the synod excommunicated four leaders: Instantius, Salvianus, Helpidius, and Priscillian. Ithacius took charge of enforcing the decrees, but failed to bring the heretics to terms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-probabilism:
Probabilism is the moral system holding that, when only an act's lawfulness is in question, one may follow a solidly probable view favouring liberty, even if the other view is more probable. When a banning law is certain, its subjects must shun the banned act, unless an ordinary excuse frees them. When no law bans an act, no duty to shun it stands. 

The safe view may be more probable than the liberty view, which still keeps solid probability.
