Probabilists insist the liberty view must rest on solid proofs, not flimsy reasons too weak to win prudent men's assent. For probabilism, the Church's long tolerance and approval in St Alphonsus show it is no false moral system. Were it false, it would gravely harm the faithful's spiritual life by licensing banned acts, and the Church could not tolerate or approve it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-protestantism:
Protestantism gets a full-scale survey here, laid out under eleven heads. The heads run from the origin of the name to the movement's present state. The name itself comes from the protest lodged at the Diet of Speyer in April 1529. Princes and cities objected to a decree that would have enforced the earlier Worms settlement against reform. Three core principles anchor the survey. They are the Bible as supreme authority, justification by faith alone, and the priesthood of all believers.

Later sections test those principles in practice. They weigh private judgment, the spread of the new churches, and claims about progress in church life, civil society and religious toleration. Written from a Catholic standpoint, the piece argues its case at length. It names fair-minded Protestant historians, Creighton and Gardiner, among its recommended reading. It suits anyone wanting the Catholic Encyclopedia's reasoned account of the Reformation and its heirs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-psycho-physic:
Psycho-physical parallelism holds that mind and body run side by side without acting on each other. This encyclopedia entry states the doctrine plainly: every mental change matches a matching change in the nerves, and every brain state matches a mental state, in strict point-for-point pairing. Interaction is denied. At most, a given nervous process always brings one definite mental process with it, and a given conscious process always brings its brain state.

The doctrine rests on the claim that all mental life presupposes physical processes in the nervous system as a necessary condition. Critics answer that this need not rule out the mind's influence, since mind might still steer material energy while the physical laws hold. Fechner, Mach, Boltzmann, Höfler and von Hartmann all conceded that point. The entry weighs both sides, warning that absolute independence of the physical world would leave consciousness an unsolved riddle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pusey-and-pus:
Edward Bouverie Pusey, born at Pusey House, Berkshire, on 22 August 1800, died at Ascot Priory on 16 September 1882. He was a divine of the Established Church of England, a patristic scholar, a voluminous writer, a preacher and a controversialist. The Catholic revival among Anglicans took its nickname, Puseyite, from him. His family was of Huguenot descent. Schooling at Mitcham from 1807 and Eton from 1812 led him to Christ Church, Oxford, in 1819.

Newman's conversion to the Catholic Church in October 1845 stunned Pusey, but their friendship survived, even through years when letters stopped. The task of defending Prayer Book doctrine then fell to Keble and Pusey. They faced assaults from Catholics, Evangelicals and Broad Churchmen alike. Both allowed the Roman primacy yet insisted on the independence of local churches. His work on the Book of Daniel, the entry notes, still offers the best defence of traditional views on that book.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pyrrhonism:
Pyrrhonism is a system of scepticism founded by Pyrrho, a Greek philosopher who died in 270 BC. This encyclopedia entry admits that very little is known about Pyrrho himself. His best-known disciple was Timon of Phlius, called the sillographer, the writer of satirical verses. Pyrrho's doubt ran so deep and wide that the word Pyrrhonism sometimes serves as a plain synonym for scepticism itself.

Three claims frame the school. First, all dogmatists, philosophers who hold that truth and certitude can be reached, were mere sophists, deceiving themselves and others. Second, certitude cannot be attained, since our faculties may deceive us. Third, nothing is in itself good, beautiful, or large — nor evil, ugly, or small; or rather, things are both at once. Zeller, Turner and older dissertations on Pyrrho and Timon supply the entry's sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pythagoras-an:
Pythagoras, Greek philosopher and mathematician, founded the Pythagorean school and flourished about 530 BC. This encyclopedia entry warns that little is certain about his life. Later biographies from the first Christian centuries abound, but material from nearer his own time is scanty. He was probably born at Samos about 550 or 560 BC, travelled to Magna Graecia in southern Italy about 530, founded his school there, and died at Metapontum in Sicily.

Tales of his inventing the musical scale, working miracles and uttering prophecies belong to legend, with no firm historical root. His school's later thought turns on numbers. First to see that natural events, above all the heavens, can be stated in mathematical formulas, the Pythagoreans claimed numbers are not mere symbols but the very stuff of reality. The point is one, the line two, the surface three, the solid four, and fate, ruling human life, seven.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quietism:
Quietism, from the Latin quies, quiet, names in its widest sense a doctrine of man's highest perfection as a kind of self-annihilation. This encyclopedia entry describes the soul in quietude as wholly inactive. Thinking and willing for itself cease; it stays passive as God acts within it, absorbed into the Divine Essence. The entry calls this a false or exaggerated mysticism, dressed as lofty spirituality, yet fatal to morality if followed through.

Narrower Quietism marks the mystical strain in various sects. Condemned propositions show its shape. Sensible devotion is dismissed as self-seeking, and every felt effect in prayer is called abominable. Neither preparation before Communion nor thanksgiving after it is required, beyond passive resignation. True perfection, the entry closes, points the other way: earnest labour for God's glory, thorough obedience to lawful authority, and firm mastery over sensual impulse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rabbi-and-rab:
Rabbi and Rabbinism traces how teachers of the Law rose to power in Palestine after the Restoration. This encyclopedia entry begins with the Temple and its priesthood, whose prestige the reform of Esdras soon overshadowed. Authority passed to the Law itself, and with it to the Scribes, the Sopherim, who expounded the Law. At first scribe meant only scrivener. Since the man who copies the Law knows it best, the word grew to mean its most qualified teacher.

Knowledge of the Law became the road to fame and popularity, with Esdras himself as the model of the ready scribe. Mishna means repetition of the Law, drawn from the Tannaite repeating doctors. A baraitha is an early saying left out of the Mishna, gathered into the Tosephta or the Gemara. Mishna with Gemara forms the Talmud, teaching of the Law, divided into halaka, customary law, and agada, information about the Law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rationalism:
Rationalism, from the Latin ratio, reason, carries three senses in this encyclopedia entry. In its exact sense it names a moment in German Protestant thought. In its broader and usual sense it covers the view that human reason, or understanding, alone supplies and finally tests all truth. Occasionally it also names a method: treating revealed truth theologically by casting it into reasoned form and working it out with philosophical categories.

The German school of theological rationalism fills the first section, with its critics and its drift towards new philosophies. Schleiermacher, a contemporary of Fichte, Schelling and Hegel, helped subvert rationalism through his own religious thought, and the movement may be said to end with him. Teller called him the greatest theologian the Protestant Church had known since the Reformation. Histories by Stäudlin, Tholuck and Benn close an entry that maps reason's claims over faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-relativism:
Relativism is any doctrine that denies absolute values, either everywhere or within some limited field of being. One form holds that we know only difference or change, as Hobbes, Bain, Höffding, and Wundt taught. A second makes truth relative. Judgments mean nothing alone, shifting until they fit one system of truth, in Joachim and the Hegelians. Or truth is a property of ideas that helps us cope, for the Pragmatists. A third, Martineau's, makes moral worth relative, emerging only when motives clash.

The entry tests these claims against the absolutist case that things can be known as they are. It weighs an argument that the thing as it exists is not the thing as it is known. It answers Forsegrive's reasoning, and follows Taylor and Bradley on the relativity of reality.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-ind:
Religious indifferentism names the theories that deny man's duty to worship God by believing and practising the one true religion. It differs from political indifferentism, a state's policy of treating all faiths equally before the law. It also differs from religious indifference, the conduct of people who neglect religious duties whether or not they believe in them. Absolute indifferentism covers philosophic systems that reject the very foundation of all religion.

The entry also tracks a softer compromise born of division. As Protestant bodies split and quarrelled within themselves, some leaders sought harmony in the claim that Christianity's essentials reduce to a few great simple truths plainly stated in Scripture. Newman is quoted on the universal solvent dissolving religious establishments, and the entry weighs this minimizing theory against the Catholic claim that truth cannot be trimmed to agreement.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ritschlianism:
Ritschlianism was a conception of Christianity widely held in modern Protestantism, founded by the theologian Albrecht Ritschl. Born at Berlin in 1822, Ritschl studied at Bonn and Halle. He passed through the influence of Nitzsch, Muller, and Tholuck, and found a home in the Tubingen school of Ferdinand Christian Baur and the philosophy of Hegel. He later broke with Baur and withdrew his early theory about Luke's Gospel. At Gottingen from 1864 he taught his path.

His system centres on the doctrine of justification, approached through Kantian theory. Religious knowledge, for Ritschl, differs wholly from scientific knowledge: it is not won by theoretical insight but grows from faith bound up with practical and moral interests. What God is in himself matters less than what God is for us. Metaphysics is banished from theology. Divine justice itself ends in love, and the world serves as the means for establishing the Kingdom of God.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roman-catechi:
The Roman Catechism stands apart from other outlines of Christian teaching in two ways. It was written chiefly for priests with care of souls, and it carries an authority no other catechism matches. Poor systematic knowledge among clergy and neglected instruction of the faithful, with Reformers' tracts flooding every country, created the need. The Fathers of Trent therefore resolved to publish a method for teaching the rudiments of faith to all pastors and teachers.

That resolution came on 26 February 1562, at the suggestion of St Charles Borromeo. Pius IV gave the work to four theologians under three supervising cardinals. Borromeo oversaw the Italian text, finished in 1564. Cardinal Sirletus polished it, and Pogianus and Manutius turned it into classical Latin. Published in Latin and Italian at Rome in 1566, it was ordered into every vernacular as the Church's official manual of popular instruction.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rosmini-and-r:
Antonio Rosmini Serbati was a philosopher and founder of the Institute of Charity. Born at Rovereto on 24 March 1797, he died at Stresa on 1 July 1855. Schooled at home until twenty, he studied three years at Padua, then returned to Rovereto for Holy Orders. Ordained priest at Chioggia in 1821, he took a doctorate in theology and canon law at Padua in 1822.

In Rome in 1823, Pius VII encouraged him to reform philosophy. From 1823 to 1826 he studied philosophy at Rovereto, chiefly St Thomas. He lived by two maxims: never take up charity works on his own initiative, but wait for a clear sign of God's will. At any clear sign, he took up the work eagerly, without personal preference. On these maxims he based the Institute of Charity, founded in 1828 at Monte Calvario.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sabbatarians-:
Sabbatarianism denotes people or parties distinguished by peculiar opinions or practices about the Sabbath. First it means rigorists who apparently confuse the Christian Sunday with the Jewish Sabbath. Not content with banning servile work, they will not allow many ordinary occupations on Sunday. This form has chiefly prevailed among Scottish and English Protestants. Of late years it has declined, with a tendency toward laxity in Sunday rest.

These Sabbatarians never formed a distinct sect, merely a party of rigorists scattered among many Protestant denominations. Yet they share with proper Sabbatarian sects the error of neglecting the distinction between the Christian festival and the Jewish Sabbath. This development appears in Sabbatarian Socinians founded in Transylvania toward the end of the sixteenth century. Their first principle was observing the rest day with Jews on the seventh day, not on Sunday.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-simon-a:
Claude Henri de Rouvroy, Count of Saint-Simon, was born in Paris in 1760 and died there in 1825. A restless aristocrat who scorned tradition from boyhood, he fought at Yorktown in the American war and grew rich by speculation during the Revolution. Eleven months in prison followed, and then he dreamed of remaking society through science. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia pairs his wild life with the school that took his name.

Trusting scholars and industry rather than soldiers and priests to regenerate the world, he imagined a united Europe with shared institutions, and a society run by administrators instead of commanders. Aided first by Thierry and then by the young Auguste Comte, he published plans for European reorganisation and a new moral code. The entry presents him as a forerunner of socialism, ardent, impractical, and impossible to ignore.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scepticism:
Scepticism, from the Greek skepsis, looking into or doubt, can mean doubt on rational grounds, disbelief on rational grounds, or denial that truth can be reached at all. In its strict philosophical sense it means a systematic denial that the human mind can know anything with certainty, whether across all knowledge or only in some field. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia draws careful boundaries.

Scepticism differs from agnosticism, which denies only metaphysics and natural theology, and from positivism, which denies knowledge beyond laws linking phenomena. It differs from atheism too, since the atheist denies God's existence, not our power to know whether He exists. The entry then recounts sceptic thinkers from Pyrrho through Hume to modern writers, answering each school in turn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-schism:
Schism, from the Greek schisma, a rent or split, means in theology and canon law the breaking of church unity. It may be the act by which a believer cuts, so far as he can, the ties binding him to the Church's social body. It may also be the state of separation that follows. Its long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia starts from Paul's plea to Corinth that no schisms divide them.

Paul elsewhere pictures believers' unity as the body's members working in harmony, tempered by God so that no schism troubles the body. The entry distinguishes schism from heresy, which denies doctrine, and from apostasy, which abandons faith, and sets out its moral character and canonical penalties. It then surveys great schisms, Eastern and Western, and the paths by which separated bodies might return.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scholasticism:
Scholasticism names both a method and a system, applied to theology and to philosophy alike. Scholastic theology stands apart from patristic theology on one side and positive theology on the other, and schoolmen themselves distinguished speculative or scholastic theology from positive theology. Its long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia lays out a thousand years of school thought in four parts.

Applied to philosophy, scholastic often marks the age between the patristic era's end in the fifth century and the modern era's start about 1450. The entry treats first the word's origin, then the period's history, then the scholastic method in philosophy with glances at theology, and last the system's contents. Neo-scholasticism's modern revival is left to its own article, and readers get a map of the whole field.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-secularism:
George Jacob Holyoake coined the word secularism around 1846. He meant an outlook that judged questions only by what this life can test. This Catholic Encyclopedia entry quotes his own definitions. They put human improvement by practical means first. They treat science as humanity's available guide. They hold that doing good in the present life is good in itself, apart from atheism, theism, or the Bible.

Holyoake's career and that of Charles Bradlaugh carry the historical half of the entry. Both men filled debating halls and journals with their views. Bradlaugh fought for years to take his seat in Parliament. The entry closes with the movement's spread in Britain and America. Its American platform called for church and state to be kept fully apart.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-semiarians-an:
The Semiarians were the conservative majority among Eastern bishops in the fourth century, set against the strict Arians. More strictly, the name fits the party of reaction led by Basil of Ancyra in 358. This entry traces their middle course. Most Eastern bishops who backed the deposition of Athanasius were not Arians, yet they were far from fully orthodox. The Antioch creed of 341 was sound except for dropping the Nicene phrase of one substance.

Basil's party held that the Son was like the Father in substance, a formula the court party kept watering down. At Seleucia in 359 the Semiarians held a majority but failed. A Constantinople council in 360 condemned their formula along with the Nicene one. Exile, return under Julian, and later splits followed, until the remnant faded into the Macedonian party and the Nicene cause won out.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-semipelagiani:
Semipelagianism was a doctrine of grace taught by monks of southern Gaul around Marseilles after 428. It sought a middle path between Pelagianism and Augustinism. After disputes lasting over a hundred years, the Council of Orange condemned it as heresy in 529. This long entry explains that the name itself was unknown in antiquity. It was coined around 1590 in a later dispute, then kept as a handy label for the early heresy.

The monks, led by John Cassian of Saint Victor, accepted original sin and the need for grace. They thought Augustine went too far on prevenient grace, the grace that comes first. Cassian argued from Scripture that God often waits for a good impulse of the natural will before helping it. The entry follows the quarrel through Prosper of Aquitaine, papal letters, and later councils to the final condemnation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-shamanism:
Shamanism is a vague term explorers of Siberia used in the 1700s and 1800s. It names a form of magic or science, not a single religion, by which nature was thought to come under human control. It prevails among Turanian and Mongolian tribes and American Indians, blending with their varied beliefs. Turanians held that the heaven god Tengri created shamans to fight evil spirits for men's good. Buddhist Mongols called it the black faith.

At its base lies animism, the view of the world as alive with spirits. The shaman works as healer, earning the name medicine man, as keeper of myth and tribal wisdom, as magistrate who detects crime, and at times as war chief. His means include symbolic magic, fasting, solitude, and incantations, often in an ancient or meaningless tongue. Among Yakuts the shaman's power is graded by his animal protector, from dog to bull or eagle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sikhism:
Sikhism, the religion of a warlike sect of India, arose in the Punjab with its center at Amritsar, where its sacred books are kept and worshipped. The name Sikh means disciple, and strict observers were later called the Khalsa. The founder, Nanak, now called Sri Guru Nanak Deva, a Hindu of the Kshatriya caste, was born near Lahore in 1469 and died in 1539. Religious from childhood, he wandered across India and matured a system revolting from polytheism and caste exclusiveness.

It taught one God, salvation through faith and good works, and the equality and brotherhood of all people. The faith spread fast under nine successive gurus. Ill treatment only hardened the disciples, who took on a military character as Singhs, champion warriors. Under Gobind Singh, tenth and last guru, they took up open war against the Emperor of Delhi.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-socialism:
Socialism would replace private ownership of productive sources and distribution means with state monopoly. It would place the activities of human life under governing control. State control alone is not socialism, nor is mere revolt against inequality or any plan to banish poverty. Socialism is also a philosophy of social life, judging all human activity from an economic standpoint, born of inequalities produced by wealth concentrated in few hands.

The movement runs from older utopias through Lassalle's German Working Men's Association. It continues through the Eisenach party of 1869 under Liebknecht, Bebel, and Singer, and the Gotha programme of 1875. Repression under Bismarck only strengthened the party, which won 110 Reichstag seats in January 1912. Bernstein's Revisionism, influenced by English Fabians, then pushed the party from revolutionary Marxism toward reforms. How far its philosophical and religious tendencies prove incompatible with Christian thought and life is the closing question.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-socinianism:
Socinianism is the doctrine of an Antitrinitarian sect born of the Reformation, named for Lelio Sozzini of Siena and his nephew Fausto Sozzini. A secret society meeting at Vicenza in 1546 discussed the Trinity, and its members, broken up, mostly fled to Poland. Fausto, holding his uncle's papers, reached Poland in 1579 and gave the sect its individuality, after the Socinians had separated and settled at Racow in 1570.

Antitrinitarians deny distinction of persons in the Godhead, holding God's absolute simplicity against the Trinity and rejecting any proportion between finite and infinite that incarnation would require. Socinus made the Bible everything, interpreted by reason alone, thrusting aside mysteries reason cannot grasp. He denied original sin and Catholic justification, allowed two sacraments as mere incentives to faith, rejected infant baptism, and held the wicked are annihilated, with no hell.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-spiritism:
Spiritism is the belief that the living can and do communicate with the spirits of the dead, together with the practices used to attempt it. This long entry distinguishes it sharply from its near namesake. Spiritualism, the philosophy, holds only that a spiritual order is as real as the material and that the human soul is a spiritual substance, a far narrower claim.

Spiritism, by contrast, has taken on a religious character. It claims to prove the spiritual world that all religions presuppose and to found a worldwide faith in which old dogmas are set aside. Its spokesmen differ over Christianity and have framed no fixed creed, expecting a fuller revelation, and the entry examines those ambitions with a critical eye.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-spiritualism:
Spiritualism, in its proper philosophical sense, is the doctrine that the universe holds more than matter and its workings, and this entry sets it against materialism. The word has often been borrowed for belief in messages from the dead and the devices used to seek them. That meaning is better given to Spiritism, the term used in Italy, France, and Germany.

True spiritualism maintains real beings, minds and spirits, radically distinct from matter. It may deny material being outside mind, as in idealism, or allow the material world alongside the spiritual. Taking forms from Fichte's monism onward, it offers readers a clear statement of why mind cannot be reduced to matter, and where its arguments meet their limits.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-symbolism:
Symbolism means giving outward things and actions an inner meaning, above all for religious ideas. This long entry argues that such meaning is essential to all external worship, and that the Church borrowed freely from a common stock of significant acts known to every age and nation. Baptisms, lights, incense, flowers, unctions, and sacrifices all carry meanings beyond themselves.

Christianity claims no monopoly here, and symbols work only when natural and simple enough for ordinary minds. The Old Testament teems with them, from Genesis images of man's making to the Creed's right hand of God, and the Song of Songs demands a symbolic reading throughout. Durandus's Rationale stands as the great medieval storehouse of the subject.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-syncretism:
Syncretism comes from a Greek verb for Cretans setting aside quarrels when a foreign enemy approached, as Plutarch explains. Erasmus spread the term in the sixteenth century for dissenters holding together despite differences of opinion, above all in theology. Later writers wrongly linked it to a verb for mixing, and the inexact sense of blending incompatible things persists today.

The entry's first section treats the fusion of pagan religions. Alexander's conquests mingled Greek and Eastern cults. Rome absorbed the gods of conquered peoples until it became the temple of the whole world. Under Caracalla, Heliogabalus, and Alexander Severus, the many cults were viewed as forms of one thing. Later sections cover theological and Protestant uses of the term.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-syndicalism:
Syndicalism takes its name from French syndicats, unions of workers in one trade or industry pursuing common economic interests. The word should mean the same as industrial unionism. Like socialism, though, it has narrowed to the ideas of French syndicates joined in the General Confederation of Labour. Revolutionary unionism, anarchism, and socialism combined to form it, blending Proudhon, Marx, and Bakunin into direct action.

No careful science fused these ideas. Working side by side in the same unions, members slowly agreed on radical plans for action, while keeping their own views outside the movement. Its primary object is the destruction of the existing social order, the expropriation and abolition of capital, and the end of the whole wage system. Later sections develop its doctrines and tactics, with French sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-taoism:
Taoism is the second of China's three state religions. It draws on the philosophy of Lao-tze. Legge calls it a way of living men should cultivate as the highest and purest growth of their nature. De Groot calls it the Religion of the Tao, the path or course of the universe. In short, it is the religion of Heaven, Earth, and Nature at large, or Naturism.

Lao-tze, the Old or Venerable Philosopher, or literally Old Boy, was born in 604 BC. His birthplace was K'io-jin in Ts'u, now Honan, according to tradition. Legend says his mother carried him seventy-two or eighty-one years, explaining his white hair at birth. His family name was Li, his personal name Eul, meaning Ear. His posthumous name was Tan, meaning Flat-eared. The entry then follows Taoism into organized religion, with its priestly hierarchy and state recognition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-lamb-in-e:
Catacomb art supplies one of Christianity's oldest symbols here: the Good Shepherd bearing a lamb on his shoulders, flanked by two sheep. Eighty-eight such frescoes appeared in Roman catacombs between the first and fourth centuries. Wilpert's reading gives each figure meaning, and the entry sets it out with care.

Shoulders bear the soul of the dead, carried by the Lord into heaven. Companion sheep stand for saints already enjoying eternal bliss. An ancient prayer for the dead echoes the image, asking the Shepherd to carry the departed, receive him among the King, and grant him joy with the saints. For students of early art, it decodes a tender and frequent scene.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomism:
Thomism is the system that follows St. Thomas Aquinas in philosophy and theology. In a broad sense it means all teaching that agrees with Thomas. In a narrower sense it means the views of the Thomistic school, chiefly Dominicans, whose opinions other thinkers dispute even while claiming Thomas as their master. The entry explains this twofold use with care.

Readers find the school's history from early opposition through growth, decline and the nineteenth-century revival known as Neo-Thomism. Distinctive doctrines are set out in philosophy and theology, including the school's view of how sacraments cause grace. A long roll of eminent Thomists runs from the thirteenth century to the nineteenth, showing how one master's thought shaped Catholic schools for six hundred years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-totemism:
Totemism is the group of beliefs and customs centred on a totem, a class of natural objects held to be intimately bound to a person or clan. The word comes from the Ojibway otem, meaning a person's family or tribe, and in a narrower sense his belongings. The totem is most often an animal species, more rarely a plant, and sometimes an inanimate thing such as sun, wind or rock.

The bond forms the religious side of totemism, while the customs flowing from it form its social side. A totem may belong to one person, to a clan, or, in Australia, to a sex. The entry surveys its spread among American Indians, Australian peoples, South Africans, Polynesians and Dyaks. It weighs theories of its origin, from name-giving and transmigration to economics, the external soul, conception and guardian spirits.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-traditionalis:
Traditionalism is a philosophical system making tradition the supreme rule of certitude. It holds that human reason alone cannot know with certainty the fundamental truths of metaphysics, morals and religion. So our first act of knowledge must be an act of faith, resting on revealed authority. That revelation reaches us through society, and tradition, or the general consent of mankind, guarantees its truth.

De Bonald and Lamennais held the system in its absolute form, while Bautain, Bonetty, Ventura, Ubaghs and the Louvain school softened it. De Bonald argued that man, a social being, thinks through language, and language, with its basic thoughts, must have been given by God, since man needs words even to think. The entry then criticizes the system, asking how fallible individual reasons, added together, could yield certitude.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-traducianism:
Traducianism, from tradux, a shoot or vine branch set to root, is the doctrine that parents transmit the human soul to their child in generation. When writers distinguish terms, traducianism means the materialist view that the soul passes by the organic process itself. Generationism means the soul springs from the parental soul in a mysterious way, as the body springs from the parent's body.

Both views stand against creationism, which holds that God creates each soul directly, though all agree the first human soul came by creation. Tertullian, Apollinaris and a few others defended traducianism, while most early Fathers held immediate creation. Gregory of Nyssa, Macarius, Rufinus and Nemesius lean toward generationism. After Pelagianism the question sharpened, and Benedict XII listed soul-from-soul among errors Armenians must reject, leaving generationism opposed to church teaching.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-transcendenta:
Transcendentalism covers several uses of transcendent and transcendental, all pointing in some way beyond experience. For the Scholastics, the transcendentals are notions wider than the categories, such as unity, truth, goodness and being, which go beyond every class of things. In a loose sense any philosophy stressing intuition, mysticism or the ultra-empirical counts as transcendentalism, including the New England school.

In Kant's stricter sense, transcendent means what lies beyond experience. Transcendental means the non-empirical, a priori elements in knowledge, which do not come from experience yet apply lawfully to its data. The entry then traces later idealist forms. They run from Fichte through Schelling's Absolute, neither subject nor object, to Hegel's absolute Idea. Its essence is development through nature and spirit, being and essence, soul, law, state, art, science, religion and philosophy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ultramontanis:
Ultramontanism is a term for wholehearted and active Catholicism, so called because it looks to the pope as spiritual head. For most of Europe the pope dwells beyond the mountains, that is, beyond the Alps. The word is relative: from Rome's view, the French, Germans, and all peoples north of the Alps are the ultramontanes. In the Middle Ages a non-Italian pope was called a papa ultramontano, and the term fills thirteenth-century documents before fading after the move to Avignon.

After the Reformation the word took a new and sharper sense, marking Catholics who stressed papal authority against national churches and state control. The entry traces the term through Gallicanism, Josephism, and the nineteenth-century struggles over the pope's temporal power and infallibility. It explains what ultramontanes affirmed and what their critics charged, giving readers a guide to a label that shaped Catholic politics for centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-utilitarianis:
Utilitarianism is a modern form of the hedonistic ethical theory that makes happiness the end of human conduct. Its test for right and wrong is pleasure and pain. In John Stuart Mill's words, actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness, wrong as they tend to produce its reverse. Happiness means pleasure and freedom from pain; unhappiness means pain and loss of pleasure.

The term came into vogue only after Bentham adopted it, though its tenets run older. The entry traces the doctrine from Epicurus and Hume through Bentham and Mill, setting out its calculus of pleasures and its claims about justice and rights. It then states the Catholic critique: happiness cannot ground duty, and the theory fails to protect the innocent. A clear guide to a dominant modern ethic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-utraquism:
Utraquism was the chief dogma and one of the four articles of the Calixtines or Hussites: Communion under both kinds as needful for salvation. It was first proclaimed in 1414 by Jacob of Mies, professor of philosophy at Prague. John Hus neither authored nor expounded it. Prague required its bachelors to lecture on a Paris, Prague, or Oxford doctor, and Hus built his teaching on John Wyclif of Oxford.

Wyclif's views sank into Prague students, and after Hus was imprisoned, Wycliffite influence showed in the Hussite demand for the cup for the laity. The Councils of Constance, Basle, and Trent condemned the doctrine. The entry traces the demand's rise, the compacts that tried to settle it, and its place in Bohemian religion, a compact history of a sacramental quarrel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-voluntarism:
Voluntarism, from Latin voluntas, will, is a theory explaining the universe as issuing ultimately from some form of will. In its modern metaphysical sense it is that doctrine strictly, but in a broader psychological sense the term covers any theory giving will prominence over intellect. In that looser sense Augustine, Anselm, William of Occam, and Scotus may all be called voluntarists.

Augustine himself nowhere subordinates intellect to will: his neo-Platonism makes that impossible, and in the metaphysical order God remains essentially intelligence, the Father of Truth, in whom the Platonists' intelligible world resides. His doctrine of grace and providence does suppose a distinctive psychology of will. On it rests his peculiar proof of God's existence, repeated through his works, yet the entry insists that Augustine's God is intelligence first, and will's prominence in him is psychological, not metaphysical.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-western-monas:
Western monasticism is traced from its introduction about AD 340, when Athanasius visited Rome accompanied by two Egyptian monks, Ammon and Isidore, disciples of Anthony. Publication of the Life of Anthony some years later, and its Latin translation, spread Egyptian monasticism widely. Many in Italy imitated it, some, like Jerome, Rufinus, Paula, Eustochium, and the two Melanias, actually moving to Egypt or Palestine as better suited to monastic life. Early Italian records are scanty, so the entry turns first to Gaul, whose knowledge is fuller.

Martin, its first exponent, founded Ligugé near Poitiers about 360, then, as Bishop of Tours. A monastery outside that city where he lived as a hermit in a wooden hut, disciples soon numbering eighty dwelling in caves and huts around him, in simple Antonian monasticism. Later sections follow Benedict and his rule, the family model of autonomous houses under an abbot father.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-western-schis:
The Western Schism was the fourteenth- and fifteenth-century division that, unlike the Eastern Schism, was no real revolt against the Church's supreme authority. The Eastern division was fomented by Constantinople's patriarchs and backed by emperors, clergy, and people for nine centuries.

Gregory XI had left Avignon, restored the papal see to Rome, and died there on 27 March 1378. At once the conclave's choice mattered enormously, since it would decide whether the future pope resided at Avignon or Rome. After conferences, projects, violent discussions, interventions of civil powers. Catastrophes of all kinds, Constance in 1414 deposed the suspect John XXIII, received the abdication of the gentle, timid Gregory XII, and dismissed the obstinate Benedict XIII. On 11 November 1417 the assembly elected Odo Colonna as Martin V, and the great schism of the West ended.
darwiniana-essays-and-reviews-pertaining:
Asa Gray's Darwiniana, printed at New York in 1876, collects the Harvard botanist's essays and reviews on Darwin's theory. Gray held the Fisher professorship of natural history, and his first article reviews the Origin of Species itself. Species, variation, and artificial selection receive a botanist's definitions. Agassiz, his Harvard colleague and Darwin's great opponent, stands opposite throughout.

Design versus Necessity and Natural Selection Not Inconsistent with Natural Theology argue Gray's lifelong position: evolution by natural selection can be theistic. Later articles follow De Candolle on oaks and Falconer on elephants. Gray arranged Darwin's American reception more than any other man, defending the science and reconciling it with faith. The volume is primary evidence in the Victorian debate, written by the friend Darwin trusted with his American defence. Its calm tone is itself an argument.
doe-osti-2997177-operational-forecasting: Predicting human-caused earthquakes got its DOE forecaster, and this CRADA final tunes the warning system. The pages log the prediction trials. The geophysicists get their closeout. The quakes were induced. The trials were prediction. The closeout was geophysicist. The system was warning.
doe-osti-3018774-feasibility-and-qualita: Fuel cell buses got airport-backup-assessed, and this DOE text studies emergency power. The pages detail the risk findings. The transport folks get their data. The use was backup power. The data were transport. The power was emergency. The assessment was risk.
doe-osti-3409108-the-hawaii-meteorology-: Hawaii MET got toolkit-built, and this DOE toolkit covers meteorology energy transmission. The pages detail the Hawaii findings. The energy folks get their data. The toolkit was transmission. The data were energy. The MET were Hawaii. The transmission were toolkit.
english-literary-criticism:
English Literary Criticism, by Charles Edwyn Vaughan and edited by C H Herford, sketches how criticism grew in England. Vaughan states his aim in the preface. He will trace the development of critical method. Each phase will be illustrated by samples from its most typical writers. He has not tried, he says, to collect the most striking pieces in the literature. The last sixty years are too rich for full treatment.

One specimen of one modern writer must suffice. That writer is Walter Pater, the critic many judge the most remarkable of all. Vaughan closes the volume with Pater's essay on the painter Sandro Botticelli. A study of painting may seem a strange end for literary criticism. Vaughan defends it: modern criticism dissolves the wall between poetry and painting. The anthology runs from the earliest English critics to that border crossing.
govdocs-archive_org-VealeFJPAdvanceToBar:
F. J. P. Veale, an English solicitor and writer, published Advance to Barbarism to trace how warfare became total between Sarajevo and Hiroshima. His span runs from the First World War's opening shots to the atomic bombing of Japan in 1945.

Veale argues that modern war shed its old limits step by step, until bombing cities and killing civilians became normal practice, and he lays much of the blame on the Allied side. The book became a staple of revisionist history and is still hotly debated. It is held as an archive item, without endorsement, for readers weighing its charges.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Patriotism_Patr: Titled simply 'Patriotism,' this declassified US government document sits in the Internet Archive's govdocs set. What it says about patriotism - or who wrote it, and when - the catalog does not say. No public text has been located. A title in search of its contents.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Vandalism_Vanda: nsia-Vandalism Vandalism: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
mediaeval-socialism:
Bede Jarrett wrote Mediaeval Socialism, printed in London and New York. Jarrett was a Dominican friar, marked by the initials O.P. Seven chapters and a book list make up the short work.

An intro sets the scene, then social conditions in the middle ages. Chapters treat the communists, the schoolmen, and the lawyers of that age. Social reformers get a chapter of their own near the end. The last chapter weighs the old theory of giving alms to the poor. A full index closes the book for students who cite it. Jarrett writes as both a friar and a trained scholar.
mill-utilitarianism:
John Stuart Mill published Utilitarianism in 1863, his clear short statement of the moral theory he inherited from Jeremy Bentham and his father. The book first ran as essays in Fraser's Magazine in 1861. Mill meant it as the theory's best case, not a textbook.

The creed is simple: acts are right as they add to happiness, wrong as they add to pain. Mill answers the stock attacks: that the rule is a pig's philosophy, too cold, or too hard to use. He ranks pleasures of mind above those of body, and grounds justice in utility. The book remains the theory's standard statement.
moulton-early-zoroastrianism:
James Hope Moulton's Early Zoroastrianism appeared in 1913 as Hibbert Lectures. The Manchester scholar gives the classic English study of the prophet. Zoroaster's faith, among the oldest prophetic faiths, fills his pages.

Moulton traces the Gathas, the hymns held to be Zoroaster's own words. The stark duel of good and evil stands at the faith's core. He weighs the faith's long sway on Jews, Christians, and others. Learning sits lightly in prose a plain reader can follow with ease. Many still call the book the best first guide to the whole subject. Moulton's fairness toward a faith not his own wins trust fast.
nasa-tm-19650024111-dipole-resonances-in:
Peter A Sturrock, of Ames Research Center and Stanford's Institute for Plasma Research, studied resonances in a magnetized plasma. Radar soundings from a satellite above the ionosphere had shown such resonances. A dipole antenna can excite them and can also detect them. A plasma is resonant, Sturrock explains, when the group velocity for a mode falls to zero.

His treatment is theoretical and treats the dipole as vanishingly small. The plasma is taken as uniform, or homogeneous, throughout. Ionosphere soundings from satellites were new at the time. Explaining their odd echoes required exactly this kind of careful wave theory, tied to a real instrument in orbit.
nasa-tm-19690009834-the-sdp-3-a-computer:
R. A. Cliff of Goddard Space Flight Center describes the SDP-3, a computer built for small scientific spacecraft, in this paper. Spacecraft radios can only send limited data to Earth. Cliff argues for raising the worth of each transmitted bit instead of just sending more bits.

The SDP-3 is a general-purpose stored-program computer meant as the core of a small spacecraft data system. It processes data on board and removes redundancy before transmission. Removing redundancy in space can use less power than sending the raw data. The machine uses serial, two's complement arithmetic with sixteen-bit words. A sixteen-level priority interrupt system supports time-sharing operation aboard the spacecraft.
nasa-tm-19690025525-the-feasibility-of-w:
William J. Robinson Jr., of the Space Sciences Laboratory at Marshall Space Flight Center, wrote this revised report, TM X-53806, dated May 27, 1969. He studies the feasibility of beaming power wirelessly to an orbiting astronomical station. A station fed from outside could avoid carrying all of its own power generation gear into orbit.

Two beaming methods are worked through in full: microwaves and lasers. For each, Robinson covers power generation, transmission across space, and reception with conversion back to electricity. Overall microwave efficiencies get their own summary section. A head-to-head comparison then weighs the two methods stage by stage. Artist's drawings show the station under each kind of beam before the conclusions chapter.
paradoxes-of-catholicism:
Robert Hugh Benson's Paradoxes of Catholicism began as sermons. He preached them in England and in New York. A complete course followed in Rome, in the Lent of 1913. His preface, dated Easter 1913, warns that the pages abbreviate the sermons. Some ideas appeared earlier in Christ in the Church. He risked repetition rather than incoherency, he says.

The contents pair opposites throughout. Jesus Christ, God and Man, opens the course. The Catholic Church, Divine and Human, follows. Peace and War, Wealth and Poverty, and Sanctity and Sin come next. Joy and Sorrow, Faith and Reason, and Authority and Liberty continue the pattern. Benson, a convert and a priest, argues that the Church holds both poles of each pair at once.
plato-and-platonism: Walter Pater's Plato and Platonism reaches this library as a Project Gutenberg e-text, number 4095 in that series, produced by Alfred J. Drake. The sample held for this entry, however, contains only the Project Gutenberg header and license matter, with the title and author's name, and no pages of Pater's text itself. Because the sample shows no part of the work's actual writing, its treatment of Plato cannot be described from the evidence provided here.
podcast-dannyjones-8jksrbKGGSM:
Travis Kitchens returns to Danny Jones's podcast with a claim pitched at full volume. Billionaires, he says, are secretly funding a psychedelic holy war. In his account they bankroll the spread of mind-altering drugs as a spiritual and political project. Kitchens connects foundations, research money, and the psychedelic revival into one design.

Jones works through the money trail with him, name by name. The revival itself is real and well funded, and readers can verify its donors; the holy war framing is Kitchens's interpretation of that money's purpose. The episode keeps the two separate in presentation even when the guest merges them. For listeners tracking how psychedelics moved from counterculture to boardrooms, the conversation offers a suspicious, detailed, and arguable map of who paid for the trip.
podcast-dannyjones-JMR7_5SSWsM:
Whitley Strieber wrote Communion, the bestselling account of his own abduction experiences, and changed how America pictured aliens. With Danny Jones, the most famous abduction witness alive discusses human-alien hybrids said to live among us, and what he believes the visitors intend for humanity.

Strieber has told his story for nearly forty years, refining a theology of the encounter along the way. Jones questions him as a seeker rather than a skeptic, and Strieber answers with the calm of a man long past caring who believes him. No evidence settles his claims, and the episode offers testimony instead. Its preservation value is cultural: the founding witness of the modern abduction era, speaking at length in his own late style, for the audience that inherited his imagery.
podcast-dannyjones-j_gMP1TgFsM:
Con artist Matthew Cox joins Danny Jones for a true-crime talk billed around the Gabby Petito case. The title asks if her fiance was a psychopath. Cox knows fraud and prison from the inside.

The sample opens on Cox's own new film about a con man contest in Europe. It then turns to the Theranos trial of Elizabeth Holmes. Cox gives a fraudster's read on lies, charm, and self-belief. The Petito question frames the hour, but Cox's own past gives the talk its sharp, uneasy edge throughout. Listeners get both crime analysis and showmanship.
podcast-joerogan-cdP3L73yySM:
Commentator Hotep Jesus sits with Rogan for episode 1318 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Known for blunt online broadcasts, he brings an unfiltered take on race, culture, and the internet's wars. The talk is fiery by design, and Rogan lets it run hot.

The two argue and joke their way across the subjects that built his following, from media narratives to personal responsibility. Rogan pushes back where the claims stretch and laughs where they land. The episode preserves a provocative voice at full volume, the kind of guest booking that made the young show a free-speech landmark for its fans.
podcast-joerogan-p6LJXPOv4SM:
Robert F. Kennedy Jr. sits with Joe Rogan for episode 1999, recorded while Kennedy was running for president. Kennedy, an environmental lawyer from the famous political family, had broken with the Democratic Party. The long talk gave his campaign one of its biggest platforms.

Kennedy lays out his views on vaccines, public health agencies, and corporate power over government. He also talks about the environment and the legacy of his father and uncle, both killed in the 1960s. Rogan lets him speak at length with few interruptions. The episode became a key moment in Kennedy's run and in Rogan's political reach.
podcast-joerogan-qSLs1-KwasM:
Graham Hancock returns to the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2215 with fresh claims about a lost Ice Age civilization. Hancock, author of Fingerprints of the Gods, argues that a comet strike wiped out an advanced culture. His Netflix series made that case to millions.

Hancock updates Rogan on sites and finds he says support his theory. He attacks the archaeology establishment for refusing to debate him fairly. Rogan, his most loyal platform, lets him lay out the full argument at length. The episode shows how Hancock's once-fringe ideas now reach a mass audience first.
podcast-tuckercarlson-tFM6L6TopsM:
Political strategist Steve Bannon joins Tucker Carlson after Israel strikes Iran. Both men oppose deeper American involvement in the war. They warn the fight could split the movement that backed Donald Trump.

Bannon argues that a long war would drain support among working-class voters. Carlson agrees that foreign wars have hurt past presidents and parties. They discuss pressure from donors, media voices, and party leaders. The episode captures a sharp split inside the American right over Israel, Iran, and the limits of loyalty to Trump. Neither man hides how deep his doubts about the war run.
poems-of-american-patriotism:
Brander Matthews chose the poems for this anthology of American patriotic verse, illustrated by N. C. Wyeth and dedicated to the memory of Theodore Roosevelt. Matthews explains in his preface, first written in New York in 1882 and extended for this revised edition. That he gathered poems of feeling as well as action, since both show the temper of their times. Arrangement is chronological, so that the history of America as told by her poets unfolds in order.

Old favorites dominate, printed carefully from the best texts, with brief notes before many poems explaining the occasion that produced them. Two score years of new events forced changes for the extended edition, dropping a few lesser pieces to make room for recent commemorations. The result is a nation's story in song, from colonial daring to modern war, as its own poets chose to sing it.
poems-of-optimism:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox issued Poems of Optimism in 1913, and the London edition of 1919 from Gay and Hancock shows a book transformed by war. Her usual creed, that attitude conquers circumstance, here meets the Great War head-on. The contents open with a whole war section: Greater Britain, Belgium, Knitting, Mobilisation, and the Ghosts, poems written while Europe burned and America debated its part.

Wilcox's optimism was never mere smiling; it was a discipline she preached to millions of newspaper readers, and the war poems test it against casualty lists. Poems about the men-made gods and the poet's theme widen the lens from battle to belief. Reprinted in 1915, 1918, and 1919, the volume records how America's favorite encourager answered the worst news of her lifetime, refusing despair in public, in rhyme, on schedule.
pragmatism:
D. L. Murray wrote this short Pragmatism for the series Philosophies Ancient and Modern, with a preface by F. C. S. Schiller, the Oxford humanist who led the movement in Britain. The first chapter, the Genesis of Pragmatism, begins by mocking the newspapers' picture of the doctrine: audacious novelty. An insurgence of emotion against logic, transatlantic slang, the sordid commercialism of the Anglo-Saxon mind dressed as philosophy.

All these ideas are mistaken, Murray answers. Pragmatism is neither revolt nor revolution but evolution, a collective name for the most modern solution of puzzles that have impeded philosophy from time immemorial. As interesting to common sense as to the metaphysician. His exposition tests the doctrine against skepticism since Hume and against the part that will plays in accepting beliefs. As an introduction written while the fight was live, the book has the advantage of explaining pragmatism before the textbooks froze it.
preaching-and-paganism:
Albert Parker Fitch, professor of the history of religion at Amherst College. Delivered these lectures as the forty-sixth series of the Lyman Beecher lectureship on preaching at Yale, published by Yale University Press in 1920. The title states his provocation: the church that means to preach to a modern age must first understand how much of that age is honestly pagan. How much of its own preaching has forgotten what religion is.

Fitch had already asked whether the church can survive in the changing order, and this volume presses the question on the preachers themselves. The Cooper memorial fund, honoring a Connecticut pastor of the class of 1865, carried the lectures into print. The book belongs to the moment when American Protestantism, shaken by war and science. Debated whether to fight modernity or to baptize it, and Fitch argues for preaching that knows its audience's real creed.
sextus-empiricus-and-greek-scepticism:
Mary Mills Patrick, president of the American College at Constantinople, wrote this study as a thesis taken for a doctor's degree at the University of Bern in November 1897. Deighton Bell issued it at Cambridge in 1899. A list of German studies of Sextus by Pappenheim opens the scholarly frame.

Patrick pairs her study of Greek doubt with her own English version of the first book of Sextus Empiricus's Pyrrhonic Sketches. Sextus set out the sceptics' way of withholding assent from all claims. Readers meet both a careful account of that school and a primary text in which its method speaks for itself.
the-essence-of-buddhism:
The Essence of Buddhism, pocket series number 325 from E. Haldeman-Julius at Girard, Kansas, copyrighted in 1922, is a Buddhist anthology. Its preface praises the plan: cut and uncut jewels of wisdom, compassion, and human brotherhood, culled from many Buddhist sources by Mr. Bowden. One such gem worn on the heart, the preface says, would enrich a day.

Bowden disclaims any full corpus of doctrine or morals. Short texts and tales let new readers taste the faith in cheap, plain form. The ten-cent format put world religion in a coat pocket.
the-heavenly-father-lectures-on-modern-a:
Ernest Naville, late professor of philosophy in the University of Geneva, wrote The Heavenly Father, lectures on modern atheism. The book was translated from the French by Henry Downton, M.A., English chaplain at Geneva, and published in Boston in 1867. A quoted line states the aim: to oppose error with faith in God as given by the Gospel, faith in the Heavenly Father.

The preface explains that the lectures were first delivered at Geneva and then at Lausanne, before two audiences that together numbered about two thousand five hundred men. Portions taken down in shorthand ran in a Swiss review. Readers in other countries then sought translations, and proof sheets were sent out as the work came from the press.
the-inhumanity-of-socialism:
Edward F. Adams joined two papers in this volume. One was read at the University of California in 1913. The League of the Republic heard it there. An earlier one went to the Ruskin Club of Oakland. His foreword concedes a hard point. A lifetime of writing on socialism would say nothing new. Each new age still wants fresh statements, he argues. Old texts do not satisfy new readers.

His own position is absolute. Socialism is inhuman, he argues. It saps the vigor of the human race. It lulls strugglers into sloth. It stops enterprise and rewards poor work. It breeds hatred and checks production. It feeds the poor hopes that cannot come true. His closing motto urges respect for law. It praises regard for the rights of others. It counsels contentment with the simple life. The book is a period piece of American argument.
the-junior-classics-volume-7-stories-of-: Volume seven of The Junior Classics covers Stories of Courage and Heroism. William Patten selected the set, Charles W. Eliot wrote its introduction, and William Allan Neilson supplied a reading guide. A picture of Catherine Douglas fronts it, thrusting her arm through a door's empty staples. Only the title pages and first contents page are present here. The stories themselves do not appear. The list opens with Beatrice Harraden on Phidias. Charlotte M. Yonge treats Thermopylae and Regulus. Saint Genevieve follows. Jacob Abbott covers Caesar crossing the Rubicon.
the-practice-and-theory-of-bolshevism: Bertrand Russell's The Practice and Theory of Bolshevism was first published in London by George Allen and Unwin in November 1920 and reprinted in February 1921. The front pages shown here carry a transcriber's note, the title page, and the contents. Part I, on the present condition of Russia, lists chapters on what is hoped from Bolshevism and on general characteristics. A chapter on Lenin, Trotsky, and Gorky follows, then art and education. The part closes with communism and the Soviet constitution. The chapters themselves are not shown.
the-soul-of-man-under-socialism:
An essay on socialism and individual freedom, printed in London by Arthur L. Humphreys, argues that the chief gain from socialism would be release from the sordid necessity of living for others. A transcribed note credits the text to a Humphreys edition, and no author's name is printed on the title pages present here.

The writer concedes that rare figures such as Darwin, Keats, Renan, and Flaubert managed to stand apart and perfect what was in them, to the world's lasting gain. Most people, though, spoil their lives through exaggerated altruism, moved by surrounding poverty and starvation. Their well-meant remedies, the essay charges, merely prolong the disease they hope to cure, beginning with attempts to solve poverty by keeping the poor alive.
the-story-of-mormonism-and-the-philosoph:
James E. Talmage, a doctor of science, wrote these two linked works, and the publishers' preface from Salt Lake City, dated March 1914, explains their history. The Story began as lectures. Talmage delivered them at the University of Michigan, Cornell University, and elsewhere. They were first printed in the Improvement Era as a report of the lectures. A booklet from the Millennial Star office in Liverpool followed.

A revised edition from the Bureau of Information in 1910 recast the lecture style into ordinary essay form, and this third American edition is revised and amplified again. The Philosophy began as a lecture before the Philosophical Society of Denver, and translations of both works had already appeared in Swedish, Greek, Russian, Danish, and German in response to steady demand.
unitarianism:
W. G. Tarrant wrote this short history of Unitarianism, printed at London in 1912. His contents trace the movement in two lands. Early chapters cover the Unitarian martyrs of England, the old nonconformists, and the tracts that spread the cause. A New England section runs from the years before the Great Awakening to the liberal reaction that followed it.

Later parts take up the legal recognition of English Unitarianism, questions of inheritance of chapels and funds, and the modern movement's communities, ideas, and teaching methods. Tarrant opens by explaining his key terms. He says the chief issue between Trinitarians and Unitarians comes first, so that a reader can follow the history with the main dispute clear in mind. The book serves as a compact map of a small church with a long past.
what-is-darwinism: Only the title page and contents list are shown here, so Hodge's argument itself does not appear. Charles Hodge of Princeton wrote What Is Darwinism?, printed in New York in 1874. The contents open with the weight of the question. He then sets out views on how the world and living things began, naming scriptural, pantheist, and Epicurean views. Herbert Spencer gets his own part. Later parts turn to Darwin's theory, natural selection, and what Darwin means by the word natural.
